Want Headphones Built for Real Workouts? These 9 Survived Runs, Jumps, and Gym-Bag Chaos

📅 25 May 2018 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Sources indicate that listening to a hyped-up playlist can make all the difference in your workout.
  • Recent findings suggest that I used to constantly fiddle with headphones that didn’t fit right, which is a real motivational buzzkill, and once spent 10 minutes trying to hunt down an earbud that popped out mid-run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that listening to a hyped-up playlist can make all the difference in your workout. As a fitness writer and longtime distance runner, I’ve seen firsthand how the right headphones can make or break a workout. And I’ve worked my way through a range of workout headphones before I found the ones I don’t want to be without.

Recent findings suggest that I used to constantly fiddle with headphones that didn’t fit right, which is a real motivational buzzkill, and once spent 10 minutes trying to hunt down an earbud that popped out mid-run. (I never recovered it.) I’ve also discovered that some headphones are better for certain types of workouts over others. Case in point: My go-to headphones for strength training at the noisy gym are different from what I reach for when it comes to HIIT and running.

No matter the style and fit you prefer, elements like sweat resistance, battery life, sound quality, and adjustability are crucial, too. And, while I love a good bargain, I’ve learned that you can’t just grab any random pair of cheap headphones or earbuds and expect them to do the job well. After multiple rounds of testing, these are the best wireless workout headphones to consider.

In a recent development, the Apple AirPods Pro have always been a reliable pair of headphones for me, and the latest third generation is even better. Whether I’m biking or struggling through heavy reps, it delivers a premium experience, including impressive sound and a comfortable fit. And the latest edition further proves their God-tier status: heart rate, step, and calorie tracking.

In a recent development, it has a sensor that deciphers your pulse through your ear canals, which then calculates calories burned based on heart rate. I like to keep tabs on my heart rate during high-intensity cardio, so it’s a great alternative to wearing a fitness tracker. Just make sure the fit is right to get an accurate reading (four silicone ear cup sizes are available).

It also has motion sensors that can track your steps. All data transfers to the Apple Health app, so you need to own an iPhone or iPad. Luckily, I recently converted (sorry, Android).

When I’m grinding hard at the gym, I want to hear nothing around me except my hype house music. The active noise cancellation drowns out any grunters, loud gym music, TVs, and general unnecessary background noise. I feel like it’s just me and my music, so that I can laser-focus on the task at hand.

But when I need to maintain awareness during outdoor runs, I turn on transparency mode to hear oncoming traffic and people nearby. I also like that it automatically lowers my music when it detects me talking to someone. It has an IP57 rating, meaning it’s sweat and dust-resistant, and can be submerged in a meter of water for up to 30 minutes in case of any accidental puddle drops (been there). As someone who sweats a lot, each bud repels moisture very well and doesn’t fall out of my ears when jumping or running. Plus, sweat never clogs my ears—something I experienced with regular AirPods. Battery life could be better for all-day wear, but it’s good for workouts (assuming you’re not working out all day). I hit the gym after work, and the power is always drained after an eight-hour day. On the flip side, it’s easy to juice up in 15 minutes with the charging case (it offers up to 30 hours of battery life per charge). To fully restore the battery, make sure to charge overnight. Read More: Best Fitness Trackers.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones are an absolute treasure. I own a lot of headphones, but the sound quality always keeps me coming back for more. The over-ear design completely covers my ears, providing A-grade noise cancellation at prime-time hours.

The sound is immersive with balanced, deep bass that doesn’t feel piercing—an problem with lower-quality headphones I tested. I blast my tunes at full volume when getting in the zone, and I never feel uncomfortable.

Industry observers note that they look bulky, but looks can be deceiving. They never budge, even when speed walking at an incline or doing fast-paced plyometric drills. I’ve worn it during box jumps and ice skaters, and it stayed put.

Just note it’s not water resistant for intense cardio like spinning and running, where you’ll work up a sweat—although the plush padding rimming the headband and ear cups can easily be wiped clean.

Like the Apple AirPods Pro 3, I have to charge it daily in the included case, so make sure to keep the cable on hand for quick power-ups.

Read More: The Best Slim Fitness Trackers.

Sources indicate that if you really just can’t with the possibility of your earbuds falling out, but still want a compact option, Dr. Dre delivered just what you need: the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. It has hooks that seamlessly glide over the ears, ensuring a proper fit that stays put. And compared to the previous iteration that launched six years ago, it’s now smaller and lighter, and shares many of the same features as the AirPods Pro 3 (Apple does own Beats, after all), including active noise cancellation, transparency mode, and heart rate monitoring through the Beats app.

In a recent development, I’ve put it to the test during long runs, sprints, low-impact biking, and strength training. The verdict? It performs as sleekly as it looks. The sound is crisp and rich, while the bass is heavy without being overbearing.The sweat resistance is a notch below AirPods with an IPX4 rating, meaning it can withstand light rain but can’t be submerged. I’ve gotten caught in the rain one too many times while wearing these—yet, the sound quality is still the same as it was straight out of the box. And battery life is actually slightly better than AirPods, offering up to 45 hours with the charging case.However, this pair feels more uncomfortable than the Apple AirPods Pro 3. The material feels a little too hard for my liking. If you plan on walking or running for hours, the best overall is the way to go.

Industry observers note that the last thing you want is uncomfortable headphones when in the midst of PRing your next barbell squat. Working out is tough enough, so having a pair that’s übersoft will take away some of the pain. Meet the Sony WH-1000XM6—a splurge that’s worth the investment.

Thick foam on the ear cups feels like lying on a pillow, while it also seals sound better for superior noise cancellation. The wide headband is plush and fits securely onto the head without being too tight. MH senior gear and commerce editor Ryan Brower throws it in his gym bag whenever he has strength training on deck. He also appreciates the adjustable smooth slider for a custom fit, calling it a fluid mechanism.

Industry observers note that the headphones use 12 microphones to isolate and cancel out sound to deliver an immersive listening experience. Vocals and instruments sound balanced and rich, with Brower calling the sound quality superb. Battery life can run for up to 30 hours, while just three minutes of charging can provide three hours—perfect if you’re in a rush to hit the gym.

Brower’s only gripes are the lack of sweat resistance for high-intensity activities, like running or spinning, and that it feels a little bulky. So, he reserves it for less strenuous pursuits.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re into an over-ear design in headphones, you know they can get hot and sweaty fast. But the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones feel surprisingly breathable on—for an over-ear headphone. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

These headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can quickly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

The Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A massive draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

It has been revealed that I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

Sources indicate that the earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an glitch with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

Some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

Industry observers note that these earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

The earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

It has been revealed that if you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

The strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

The sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an problem since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

It has been revealed that if blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I swiftly need it before a run.

According to recent reports, full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” says Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

Sources indicate that having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

Industry observers note that for example, the total playtime for the fresh Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

You have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this issue. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

Industry observers note that A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

As a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

Industry News: Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.
  • Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women.
  • It has been revealed that GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

It has been revealed that GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In a recent development, in the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she mentioned.

In a recent development, it is notable to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sources indicate that sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is vital for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”.

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

It has been revealed that “Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve key aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

Recent findings suggest that “For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence presently available,” she noted.

In a recent development, “It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”.

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

In a recent development, one baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest indicated off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

“This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are presently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

According to recent reports, tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

It has been revealed that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Back in the day, a sweatsuit was all about comfort. It wasn’t so much a fashion staple, but the kind of thing to throw on and lounge in. With Y2K style back in vogue, matching sweatsuits are more commonplace than ever—just with a little less sparkle than the ones previously sported by icons like Paris Hilton and J.Lo in the early 2000s. And, with the rise of athleisure, these simple sweats have gotten the luxury treatment: they’re softer, more flattering, and pricier than ever.

Whether you’re the kind of person who considers it a cozy wardrobe essential, or you’re just looking to treat yourself to something comfortable to wear around the house, there have never been more choices when it comes to the best matching sweatsuits. Since we’re heading into winter (and Black Friday is just around the corner!), Women’s Health editors tested the most popular styles.

Here are our thoughts on the matching sets after months of lounging in them, working from home in them, and even wearing them to work.

Oner Active Foundations Zip Up Hoodie.

Oner Active Foundations Sweatpants.

In a recent development, oner Active’s workout clothes have had our hearts at WH for a while. That’s why we were excited to put their loungewear to the test. Associate Health and Fitness editor Addison Aloian wore this set while traveling, chilling at home, and even working behind the scenes on a photoshoot.

According to recent reports, “I absolutely love this set from Oner,” she states. She loves it for its comfort, warmth, and versatility (Aloian says she knows she could wear it outside in the chilly NYC winter, layer it under her ski clothes, or pop it on over leggings for her warm-up at the gym). “But the standout feature is the color,” Aloian says. “So many sweat sets are gray or black, but the turquoise is stunning and makes it a standout in my closet when I want a monochromatic moment.” She opted for the “oil blue” color, but Oner also has options like alpine green and toasted red, plus your neutral staples.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also one of the more affordable options we tested—and on sale for half off this Black Friday. But that doesn’t mean it skimps on quality: The material feels super plush since it’s made from 67% cotton and 33% polyester, for a super plush feel that doesn’t pill or shed after one wash.

In a recent development, the set’s one flaw? The bottoms are a little long. At 5 '1, Aloian claims she’d love a “short” option as well. Oner does offer a “long” length, though, for the taller girlies.

Old Navy Bounce Fleece Half-Zip Pullover Sweatshirt.

Old Navy High-Waisted Bounce Fleece Jogger Sweatpants.

Industry observers note that in a world of expensive sweat sets, Old Navy’s Bounce Fleece line provides a budget-friendly—and stylish—option. “You’d never know these are super affordable,” says Fitness editor Cori Ritchey. They hold their own with the rest of the pricier sets from their fit to their feel.

The highlight for Ritchey is the material, a mix of polyester, rayon, and spandex. “It moves with you, and the fabric feels like it breathes compared to other sweatsuits that feel too heavy and hot.” One small caveat: Be sure to follow the wash instructions and keep your cycle on cold and gentle, tumble dry low, and keep the garments inside out. Ritchey indicates she noticed a bit of pilling after the first wash, but says that after following the wash instructions during the next few washes, the set stayed in great shape.

Industry observers note that the half-zip and jogger combo makes for a put-together look and is cozy enough for traveling, running errands, or lounging around the house, Ritchey indicates. The set comes in plenty of neutral colors, plus some fun ones like orchid. It’s also the first on our list that doesn’t have a prominent logo, for anyone who wants a clean-looking set with no branding. Another point for Old Navy: It’s the most size-inclusive on the list. Sizing goes from XS to 4XL, with regular, tall, and petite options.

Alo Accolade Crew Neck Pullover.

Sources indicate that alo is another longtime favorite at WH. The brand is known for its cozy, stylish (and premium-priced) loungewear. The fit is what we love most. The set, which comes in over a dozen colors, has an oversized feel, yet still manages to look intentional, indicates Deputy Features editor Carina Hsieh. “Unlike other sweatsuits, this one doesn’t look or feel unflattering or sloppy,” she says. She especially likes how it falls on her shoulders.

In a recent development, it’s also the “perfect transition-weather sweatsuit.” The French terry material is made up of 65% cotton and 35% polyester, for a “really soft, thick, and high-quality” feel. The fabric doesn’t feel ultra-heavy, though, so it’s a great pick for fall and spring when you might overheat in thicker sets. Another perk? The pants have pockets.

However, the sizing isn’t the most intuitive. Hsieh, who is typically a small or medium in other brands, is an extra-extra small in these pants. The pants also run a bit long. Hsieh says sizing down is likely the way to go for this set.

Aritzia Cozy Sweatfleece Mega Funnel Neck.

Aritzia Cozy Sweatfleece Mega Jogger.

Industry observers note that I had been hearing great things about Aritzia’s Sweatfleece line, and after testing for over a month, I can attest that it’s truly the coziest sweat set I’ve worn. Made from 78% cotton and 22% polyester, the material is soft with a fleece-lined interior. They’ll definitely keep you warm; that fleece inside is perfect for chilly temps. But they don’t feel too heavy. The material is still breathable, and I don’t get overheated when I’m wearing them.

I also love the look of this set, especially with the funnel/mockneck style—which is very on-trend. I have been wearing the suit when I work from home, and it makes me feel put together and chic, even though I’m in the coziest clothes I own. I’m also a runner, and I've noticed that this is the first thing I want to put on after I shower post-run. It’s the ultimate comfy outfit for recovery.

According to recent reports, when it comes to sizing, these sweats have a “mega” fit, which means they’re oversized. I still sized up just to make sure mine would be roomy, but learned that I didn’t need to. These give you an oversized fit at your true size. Plus, as a shorter girlie (5’2!), I was thrilled that they came in short, regular, and long lengths. They’re still just the tiniest bit long, so I flip the elastic on each ankle under to shorten the legs. You can’t tell a thing!

Set Active Staple SET Uniform Layered Crewneck.

Set Active Staple Straight Leg Sweatpants.

This vintage-inspired sweatsuit from Set Active is made from 100% cotton, for those who want to prioritize more natural fibers. “I love how soft they feel,” Hsieh says. “Sometimes 100% cotton feels stiff to me, and I’ve found that cotton sweats in particular lay weirdly at the chest when they’re oversized, but these maintain their plushy softness.”.

This set is mid-weight, cozy, and warm. “I love a crewneck and sweatpants to sleep in, but sometimes find other sweats to be too much underneath my many layers of comforter and other blankets. These are the perfect weight to be warm and let me sleep comfortably,” Hsieh notes. The crewneck isn't too bulky either—a challenge for a lot of sweatshirts—and fits easily underneath a jacket.

This set comes in tons of bold colorways, with contrasting collars and retro logos on the crewneck—so it’s great for anybody who's into the vintage activewear look. The only con? Hsieh, who is 5’3, found that pants run slightly long.

lululemon Scuba Oversized Full-Zip Hoodie.

lululemon Scuba Mid-Rise Wide-Leg Pant.

This lululemon hoodie was named the best zip-up in our guide to the best hoodies for its comfy, classic fit. Where the hoodie shines, according to Associate Style & Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz, the pants are just as impressive. Both stand out for the waffle material: A soft, stretchy blend of cotton, modal, and polyester. She finds it more breathable than some of her buttery-smooth cotton sweats. Another perk? It’s basically immune to pilling.

“Both pieces are incredibly soft and cozy,” Zitz states. “I love the slightly oversized, waist-length fit of the top. It pairs really well with the matching sweatpants, which are equally comfy and have a flattering drape with a straight-leg fit.”.

This set styled with a plain white tee underneath and a pair of comfortable sneakers “happens to be my travel fit of choice,” she indicates. “The hoodie keeps me warm and cozy during cold flights and early morning departure days, but I can easily unzip it or tie it around my waist if I get too warm.”.

Vuori Restore Straight Leg Sweatpant.

The Restore hoodie is one of Vuori’s best sellers, and for good reason. “I love the material,” Richey says. “It’s very soft and feels super durable.” The French terry material (a cotton blend that’s smooth on the outside with brushed fleece on the inside)is made of breathable cotton and sturdy polyester.

Recent findings suggest that as far as sweat sets go, this one has a lot of heft. The Restore line is thicker and denser than the label's BlissBlend or DreamKnit lines, making this set incredibly warm with a high-quality, structured feel. “The softness seems to also stay wash after wash, which is a huge win!” Richey adds.

When it comes to fit, the hoodie has a perfectly oversized shape, but you might benefit from sizing up in the bottoms, particularly if you’re thicker-thighed, Ritchey notes. The pant comes in short, regular, and long lengths, giving you even more options to find the right fit.

This Spanx set stands out as a lighter-weight and more polished option. “This set feels so light and airy,” says Zitz. Spanx’s Air Essentials is made of their signature Spacer Fabric (a blend of modal, polyester, and elastane), for an ultra-smooth feel with plenty of stretch.

“It’s one of the most comfortable lounge sets I own, but also one of the nicest looking,” Zitz notes. The structured half-zip top and tailored (yet roomy) wide-leg pant have an almost dressed-up look, so you can wear the set to lounge or out of the house. It also comes in nearly 20 colors—a range of neutrals to bright options like red, blue, and plum.

In a recent development, there is one downside: Neither the top nor bottom has pockets. While they might take away from the streamlined look, being able to slip your phone or wallet into a small pocket would be a bonus.

Gap VintageSoft Oversized Henley Pullover.

Gap VintageSoft Baggy Wide-Leg Sweatpants.

It has been revealed that gap certainly holds its own in the loungewear category. Aside from the cozy feel (thanks to a blend of cotton and polyester), it really shines when it comes to style.

It has been revealed that “I love a wide-leg sweatpant,” Zitz states. “I find they look less loungey than a jogger, and this pair is roomy without swallowing up my entire frame.” Even better is the henley top: The button-up design and mock neck make this top look more chic than your average crewneck or half-zip. “It’s unlike any other sweatshirt I own in terms of style,” Zitz says.

One area for improvement: The color options. Our tester opted for a soft blue color, but would have preferred a more neutral gray—it just wasn’t in stock due to the limited colorways.

Rhone DreamGlow Barrel Leg Pant.

In a recent development, rhone is another label that the WH fitness and style editors love. I have personally been a fan of their DreamGlow line for a while. It’s warm, but also has a sleek feel to it. There’s no heaviness to this set at all.

It has been revealed that made primarily of polyester and a small amount of elastane, the fabric also contains lyocell, a semi-synthetic fiber that helps to wick moisture away from the body, creating a slightly cooling effect. This set is ideal for anyone who runs hot or for transitional spring or fall weather. I like to wear it around my apartment on work-from-home days or as a travel outfit.

Sources indicate that this is also the set for someone who is a little sweatsuit-reluctant. The top has a slightly cropped and boxy fit, while the pants are a barrel-leg shape (a.k.a. a flared mid-leg and tapered ankle). Combined with the ultra-smooth material, this set looks less frumpy than your old-school sweat suits.

Nuclear submarine returns from record-breaking 217 days underwater

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater.
  • “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.
  • The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater. The HMS Vengeance’s seven-month deployment overtook the 205-day milestone set by the HMS Vanguard in April. But with the Vengeance crew finally back home, critics now argue the two submarines’ lengthy back-to-back voyages are causes for concern, not celebration.

“The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles. First debuted in 1998, the vessel features 16 missile tubes, each loaded with one Trident containing up to a dozen, 100-kiloton multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). The MIRV is specifically engineered to simultaneously deploy a payload of individual nuclear weapons aimed at a list of targets. The Royal Navy continuously keeps at least one Vanguard submarine at sea, which hypothetically allows the United Kingdom to still conduct nuclear strikes in the event its land-based systems are compromised during a nuclear war.

According to recent reports, vanguard submarines were originally built to host around 140 crewmembers during three-to-four month deployments. Although a 100-day excursion was once considered rare, underwater stints are now often double the length of time, forcing sailors to stack extra provisions along already cramped corridors and inside any additional nooks. The U.K. government attributes the extended missions to budgetary cuts that have dramatically slowed down the pace of multimillion-dollar vessel maintenance projects.

Deployment aboard a submarine like the Vengeance is considered one of the navy’s most psychologically difficult assignments. The nuclear sub remains underwater in total radio silence for the entire length of a patrol to keep its position secret. The vessel can travel to a depth of around 984 feet, but it may occasionally ascend to shallower waters to communicate via a transmission buoy or floating wire antenna. Crewmembers may receive a weekly, 120-word “Familygram” message, but each dispatch is previewed by naval officials. These readers retain the right to censor any bad news or information they feel may compromise sailors’ effectiveness. Regardless of what a sailor ultimately reads, they are strictly prohibited from responding.

The toll on crew is steep, but it’s particularly difficult for the women comprising roughly 10-percent of the navy. In 2022, whistleblower Sophie Brook generated international headlines after reporting a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” while serving as one of the Royal Navy’s first female submariners. In 2024, First Sea Lord Adm. Sir Ben Key called the crew misogyny “intolerable” and apologized to the growing number of women who subsequently came forward with their own stories. The Royal Navy’s investigations ultimately resulted in the firing, demotion, and disciplining of dozens of servicemen—including Key’s own termination.

Industry observers note that key’s successor, Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, stated he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for Trident crews earlier this month, while admitting the need to “improve our submarine maintenance.”.

Industry observers note that the Vanguard fleet was designed for about 25 years of service, but will likely accumulate roughly four decades of sailing by the time its first replacement is ready. That submarine, the HMS Dreadnought, isn’t expected to sail until around 2032.

#98453. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1285 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and indicated similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and indicated similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

According to recent reports, for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

Industry observers note that from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

Industry observers note that the study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own revealed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

According to recent reports, several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

In a recent development, “Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, stated that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Sources indicate that theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he mentioned.

Sources indicate that “And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

It has been revealed that strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have concerns with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

Sources indicate that “I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being notable,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

A racerback style bra, the style in which the straps meet at the back to create an X or Y shape, happens to be a sort of Goldilocks bra option that suits most sizes because they’re super customizable. As a style writer who’s tested more bras than I can count (at different weights and sizes over the years), I’ve found that racerback sports bras tend to work especially well for smaller and larger busts alike. That’s part of why racerback bras have such a loyal following: they’re supportive, comfortable, less likely to slip around, and easy to style under a variety of workout tops.

According to recent reports, this is especially true for bras with added features like underwire, molded cups, or a wider band, says Dani Read, a senior designer for luxury lingerie brand Cosabella. Adjustable straps (as opposed to fixed backs) can also help you get the right fit in a racerback, she adds. Racerback bras are a go-to style for Women’s Health’s style and fitness team, and for this guide, we’ve selected some of our favorites that we reach for again and again.

Industry News: IONNA enables Plug & Charge for Tesla, opens 22 bay site in Westminster, CA

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.
  • Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”.
  • IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IONNA, the DC charging operator backed by several major OEMs, has opened its largest DC charging site yet, with 22 bays of 400kW charging in Westminster, California.

Alongside the opening, IONNA is also enabling Plug & Charge operation for Tesla EVs, with Stellantis EVs “coming soon.”.

IONNA is a rapidly expanding DC charging network which is garnering good reviews from EV drivers, with clean, fast and easy to use charging stations (which it calls “Rechargeries”).

According to recent reports, but until now, we haven’t had all that many chargers in the LA area. There are a couple in South OC and the Inland Empire, but nothing closer to the population center of the metro area (though more are opening soon).

That changes now with IONNA’s fresh flagship charging station in Westminster. It features 12 CCS connectors and 10 NACS ports, so you can charge just about any EV (no Chademo, nor can my AC-only Tesla Roadster charge here… ho hum).

In addition to 22 chargers with peak 400kW capacity, the site features indoor and outdoor lounge space, restrooms, and other amenities like an In N Out and a taco shop across the street. (Not quite as full-featured as my favorite charging station, Rove, but IONNA has a much larger national footprint, and does have faster chargers).

Sources indicate that there’s also a small, convenience-store-like area that uses Amazon’s “just walk out” technology. You swipe a card to unlock the room, pick up any items you want, and just walk out. The many cameras on the ceiling track you (and whoever came in with you) and what you’re picking up, then charge your card for the items you took with you.

The store has snacks and drinks, though no ice cream, which is the main thing I’m looking for on a roadtrip stop… IONNA may convert one of the fridges to a freezer in the future, depending on how things go.

And, importantly, the site has trash cans and window wipers – just what you need on a roadtrip stop.

Speaking of roadtrips, the charger opening caps off a cross-country roadtrip by IONNA personnel, who set out in several cars from various parts of the country, all convening on the fresh Rechargery in Westminster.

Over 20 EVs joined the roadtrip and drove over 40,000 combined miles on their trip to Westminster. The teams charged at approximately 30% of the company’s charging sites, showing just how easy it is to do roadtrips in an EV.

The Rechargery opens tomorrow in Westminster, at 6260 Westminster Blvd, just off the 405 freeway. Look for the significant sign. For the first weeks, you can charge at a promotional rate of $0.20/kWh. Afterwards, IONNA will charge its standard rate of $0.39/kWh.

Perhaps more importantly than a new charger opening, though, is IONNA’s announcement today that Teslas can now use its network with Plug & Charge functionality (well, technically Autocharge, which is basically the same thing).

Window wipers and fluid are an underrated missing feature at EV stations, hope to see more of this.

Industry observers note that what this means is that you can link your car and credit card ahead of time (via the Presto charging app), then simply plug in at any IONNA station and start charging, without having to tap or swipe or open an app. This is similar to the experience Teslas have always had on Superchargers, so should be familiar to Tesla owners.

The functionality is rolled out across all of IONNA’s network, starting today. So you should be able to test it out on your Tesla vehicle. IONNA already supports Plug & Charge for BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Rivian, Ford, Porsche and Volvo EVs.

Further, IONNA says support is “coming soon” for Stellantis EVs (Jeep, Dodge, Ram, Fiat), stating that those cars will be able to Plug & Charge on its network in December. It now supports Autocharge for about two thirds of the EVs on American roads.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • IF YOU WANT to gain muscle, your first instinct may be to head to the gym and hit the dumbbells.
  • Resistance bands are relatively affordable, lightweight, and compact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU WANT to gain muscle, your first instinct may be to head to the gym and hit the dumbbells. And while lifting will never go out of style (in our humble opinion), we're here to tell you that's not the only way to build strength. If you're short on gear—or even just want to shake things up—it's time to add some of the best resistance bands to your training arsenal.

Resistance bands are relatively affordable, lightweight, and compact. Most importantly, they're one of the most versatile strength accessories you can buy. Adding a resistance band into your routine can be as simple as integrating it into your bodyweight warmup, or looping it onto a kettlebell to add a little extra heat to a set of swings.

"Because of the elastic properties, resistance bands recruit muscle fibers differently than free weights," explains Juan Guadarrama, CSCS, one of the creators of Men’s Health’s "7-Minute Workouts for Fat Burn".

Recent findings suggest that of course, there are tons of different types of resistance bands (and resistance band exercises) out there, from closed loop bands, thick latex bands, and bands with handles to ones that use anchors to attach to your door. Depending on the thickness, they also provide different levels of resistance, meaning that not every band workout is for light weights.

Industry observers note that we've spent years testing dozens of the best exercise bands of nearly every type and thickness. Men's Health fitness editors, in collaboration with Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative members Guadarrama and Eric Sung, CSCS (a trainer at Performance Lab in Latest York City) have compared testing notes on the best resistance bands we've tried to break down what factors set the best apart from the rest.

Industry observers note that REP Fitness’s looped bands are durable, affordable, and have a wide weight range. With resistance profiles starting as low as five pounds (3X-Light) and as high as 150 (X-Heavy), customers can gradually progress any exercise over time. They’re built with layered elastic and smoothed edges to create a smoother feel as the bands stretch and to reduce the chance of fraying (which can lead to breakage). The bands are color-coded and have the weight ranges printed clearly on each band, so I instantly know what I’m grabbing.

Marketed primarily as pull-up bands, their 38-inch length makes sense for assisted bodyweight work. However, for other moves—like curls or RDLs—that length can feel unwieldy. Still, with small adjustments, such as gripping lower on the band, double-looping the band, or widening your stance to take up slack, they function just great across a wide range of exercises.

Industry observers note that the best value comes from REP’s five-band set (2X-Light through Heavy) at $70; it’s $50 cheaper than buying each band individually. Each band includes a one-year home-use warranty (and six months for commercial use).

Read More: The Best Items For Your Gym Bag.

According to recent reports, leekey’s bands cover most bases for most folks. If you’re looking for a middle-of-the-road set of looped bands to pack in your bag for travel workouts or to help with assisted pull-ups, dips, and push-ups, this is a solid choice for under $40. The brand offers many options, so carefully review the choices before selecting. With multiple bundle options available, I think the best value is one of the five-band sets with the included door anchor.

According to recent reports, because Leekey isn’t completely transparent about the build quality, proceed with caution before pulling these toward your face or looping them over barbells for heavy pulls. A small percentage of reviewers reported snapping, though it’s unclear whether they overstretched the bands. Still, the product holds a 4.6-star average across more than 11,500 reviews. One customer even posted a photo of the purple bands draped over a barbell loaded with 405 pounds, writing: “I have been using these bands for added resistance on deadlifts and rack pulls. They are holding up well and help with adding resistance at the lockout of the pull.”.

Read More: The Best Resistance Band Workouts.

This set earns a spot for the sheer amount of resistance it offers—up to 300 pounds, more than any other kit on our list. That’s more than enough tension to challenge even advanced lifters. HPYGN also sells lighter-weight bundles at lower prices, but every option comes with the basics: a travel pouch, door anchor, handles, and ankle/wrist straps.

According to recent reports, with over 10,000 reviews and a 4.5-star average, it’s an Amazon favorite. Some users note that bands have snapped under strain or that the listed resistance feels exaggerated, though the latter is subjective. On the flip side, many reviewers praise the sturdier build. One wrote: “I was pleasantly surprised that the gear looked like the ads and worked well. I bought it because of the metal carabiners that make it easy to change bands, and I wasn’t disappointed.”.

Sources indicate that you’ll need a solid anchor point to get the most out of these, and long-term durability is a question mark. Still, if you’re trying to ditch your gym membership or want a heavy-duty band system for travel, HPYGN’s kit is a worthy pick. It’s affordable, versatile, and capable of potentially replacing machines and free weights.

This rig gives you a little more than just the bands. We put this setup to the test, and found it to be super fun and intuitive to use. You can think of the Gorilla Bow as a hybrid tool that combines the benefits of resistance bands with a bow-style bar, which allows for a lot more versatility than a resistance band alone.

In a recent development, the unique bow design accommodates up to 300 pounds of resistance (just to start, you can get heavier models) that you can use to target just about every muscle group. The bow itself is made out of aircraft aluminum while the resistance bands are double-wall latex, resulting in a durable, lightweight, and portable build.

Recent findings suggest that resistance is adjustable, with the bow supporting up to four bands at a time so you can customize your resistance to meet your needs. The set comes with one original 56-inch bow, four Gorilla Bands (10, 20, 30 and 50-pounds), a band wrap, and a 30-day all-access membership to Gorilla Bow's virtual training platform. It's pricey, yes. But it packs a lot more usability than your average standalone resistance band.

It has been revealed that mini bands are a staple for warm-ups and recovery work, often wrapped around the knees for lateral walks or used to cue better glute and abductor activation during squats. Titan’s version is a little different. Designed initially as attachments for the brand’s Vice Grip Trainer, these bands double as standalone mini bands. And because they’re built for machine resistance, they’re thicker, more durable, and provide far greater tension than typical minis.

The resistance ranges from 15 pounds up to 120 pounds, which means the lightest bands are great for activation drills, while the heavy green band can push your lateral walks well past warm-up territory.

It has been revealed that the catch is price. At nearly $50, these cost significantly more than most mini-band sets, and their uses are inherently limited compared to looped or tube bands. Still, the build quality is excellent, and the extra resistance opens the door for more challenging work than you’ll get with cheaper, flimsier bands. If you’re willing to invest once for a set that won’t wear out quickly, Titan’s mini bands are a “buy once, cry once” purchase.

Recent findings suggest that rogue is synonymous with quality in the fitness equipment space, and its tube resistance bands live up to the reputation. If you’re looking for bands to actually build workouts around—not just warm up with—these are among the best. The textured rubber handles stand out: they’re coated in a knurl-like pattern that gives you a secure grip, even when your hands get sweaty.

Sources indicate that I noted that REP Fitness’s loop bands were long at 38 inches, and Rogue’s bands clock even longer at an elastic length of 48 inches. However, the length does allow you to perform overhead presses, lateral raises, and kickbacks with the bands. To increase the tension, loop the band around a squat rack or pole and take a few steps back. (Though Rogue warns users not to overstretch the band.) Each band is a standalone product, so you can’t clip multiple elastic tubes to a pair of handles, as with other models.

Price-wise, individual bands cost a bit more than some competitors, but Rogue makes up for it with bundle pricing. A light set (bands 0-2) runs $36.50, the heavy set (3-5) is $45, and the full collection is $75. Considering the quality and the savings versus buying separately, the sets are where the real value lies. For those who want tube bands tough enough for serious training, Rogue delivers.

These resistance bands feature four tubes braided together to create a durable workout tool that can stand up to your toughest sessions. We love that consumers can choose from five resistance levels, ranging from feather-light to heavy-duty, and select the perfect size and tension based on their preferences and fitness level. We found the handles comfortable, featuring a protective sleeve and grommet reinforcement which helps to ensure a solid grip.

While they excel in mobility work, don't expect crazy heavy resistance. They come in five resistance levels, from 'very light' to 'very heavy', ranging from 3 to 27 pounds. The various levels also differ in length, ranging from the 44-inch very light cord to the very heavy 53-inch cord, so you can pick the size and tension right for you.

According to recent reports, if you want to go all in with resistance bands, WHATAFIT offers five bands (10, 20, 30, 40, 50-pound listed resistances), handles, ankle straps, a door anchor, and a carrying pouch. Some bundles even come with additional looped or mini bands. You’re not going to get much closer to having a complete gym in your home—especially for under $40—than with this set.

Recent findings suggest that the set is also wildly popular: With a 4.6-star average and over 34,000 reviews—more than any other band on this list—it has the people’s approval. You can stack the bands for more precise resistance, which makes progressive overload easier and mimics the flexibility you’d get in a commercial gym. As one reviewer put it: “The materials feel high-quality and durable, and the bands have held up really well so far. I’ve used them for upper body, lower body, and core training without any concerns. Plus, the whole set is compact and easy to store or travel with.”.

Sources indicate that what holds it back slightly is that these bands are serviceable, not premium. While natural latex is great for elasticity, it can degrade over time with sweat, sun, and repeated stretch cycles, so expect some wear. That stated, for the price, this set offers a wide breadth of use and works well for someone building up strength or who needs a versatile “one-stop” band kit.

Industry observers note that your most important consideration should be how you proposal to use your resistance bands—for solo workouts, to add resistance to exercises, to help you with dips or pull-ups, or to warm up before your lifts. No one band will perfectly check every box.

It has been revealed that most resistance bands are made from latex and rubber (or some combination of the two) and use plastic parts for accessories like handles and door anchors. (If you have a latex allergy, there are latex-free resistance bands.) So we’re not going to list materials as a significant consideration.

Likewise, the bands in this guide are all similar in price, with no major outliers. Premium and/or unique band designs cost more, but expect to pay between $20 and $70 for bands. The price scales based on the band resistance and whether or not you’re buying a set. Below are the top three things you should consider when shopping around for a upcoming resistance band.

The type of band you buy dictates the kind of workouts you can perform. Here’s a quick breakdown of the band styles you’ll see, save for a few unique models, most of which are on this list.

Also referred to as super bands, these are the quintessential resistance bands that most manufacturers sell. Because the band is a single loop, you have to get creative in performing specific exercises, but you can target most major muscles with a looped band. You can also wrap them around pull-up bars, barbells, and machines to change the resistance profile of an exercise.

In a recent development, popular in physical therapy offices, mini bands are an excellent tool for activating the smaller muscles in your hips, legs, upper back, and shoulders. They can’t support your bodyweight and they don’t stretch far enough to allow for squats, presses, or curls. Think of these as a warm-up tool, not a workout replacement.

According to recent reports, these bands are defined by a single tube of rubber with a handle on each end (usually). These bands give you the most freedom of movement, and the handles allow you to press and row more efficiently (compared to looped bands).

Recent findings suggest that some bands cite a single poundage versus a range. If a band lists its resistance as between 20 and 60 force, you’ll experience 20 pounds of resistance when the band is least stretched and 60 pounds at the most stretched position. Squatting with a 50-pound band doesn’t feel the same as squatting with a 50-pound dumbbell, either, since the force you’re resisting is literally changing with every inch you move.

Sources indicate that to track your progress effectively, find a band that has you reaching within one to three reps of failure for your desired rep range. Stick with that band until the reps feel easier, and then move up to the next heaviest band you have. Progressing with bands isn’t as easy as with free weights and machines, but you'll make gains as long as you’re basing your effort on training intensity and not weight.

It has been revealed that resistance bands can be dangerous. If they snap while doing assisted pull-ups or a face pull, you’ll fall or injure your eyes or face. No band is wear-proof, so it’s essential to use them responsibly: don’t overstretch, inspect them regularly for tears, and avoid anchoring them against textured surfaces like the knurling on a barbell, which creates friction that weakens the material.

Manufacturers use different strategies to improve longevity. Some bands are built from layered latex for added reinforcement, while others encase the elastic in a protective sleeve that reduces wear and shields the user from a whip-like snap mid-rep. These features can’t eliminate risk, but they can extend the lifespan of your bands and make training safer.

It has been revealed that as a longtime fitness journalist and NASM-certified trainer, I have spent years using resistance bands in a variety of exercise scenarios. For this story, I worked in tandem with the team at Men's Health, including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, and Fitness and Commerce Editor Charles Thorp, NASM. We also recruited the help of MH Strength in Diversity members Juan Guadarrama, CSCS and Eric Sung, CSCS to gather diverse perspectives on the topic.

Industry observers note that we used our collective experience to put together a testing pool by putting the most popular designs that we could put up against newly introduced offerings from classic brands as well as newcomers to the market. Both historically and in the pursuit of this story, we used these designs during band-only workouts, athletic movements, and to advance fundamental movements like the deadlift. The selections above represent the best resistance bands that you can buy now.

We asked Strength in Diversity member Eric Sung about his favorite ways to incorporate resistance bands with clients and in his own training.

Sources indicate that "The banded rear delt fly is great exercise to do as a warm up to prepare your body before an upper body session," says Sung. "Grab the band, hold it out in front of you, stretch it across your upper chest and try to resist the band as much and slowly as you can.".

If you're looking to get started in training lower body plyometrics, put band-assisted squat jumps on your radar. "Tie a band to a high anchor, grab each end of it, assume your squat stance, and focus on jumping as high as you can with the assistance of the band. This is a great entry point," he adds.

For more ideas, check out our list of 12 resistance band workouts you can do at home.

Similar to free weights, resistance bands help create tension and place stress on the muscles, explains Sung. However, resistance bands assist in efforts to build muscle and strength in a few unique ways.

Sources indicate that because they deliver more resistance as you stretch them further, they offer a different challenge than free weights. This means your muscles face the most load and tension at the top of every exercise. For example, the top of a resistance band pushup is a challenge; the top of a bodyweight pushup is a position of rest.

Another way resistance bands help build strength is by assisting in movements that an individual cannot yet complete at baseline standards, explains Guadarrama. "It allows athletes to move through the full range of motion and acquire neuromuscular capacity," he explains. "Over time the body can adapt, learn the movement, and build the strength needed for the unassisted effort.".

Bands can also be attached to plates and kettlebells to add more resistance to the eccentric or concentric phases of a given movement, explains Guadarrama. "Each of these methods has benefits to biomechanical advantages and providing variance in stress," he indicates.

Year after year, the Brooklinen Down Comforter has been the all-around favorite on this list for its supple texture, even weight, breathability, and easy care instructions. Beyond Brookinen’s award-winning model, we’re highlighting our full lineup of favorites in case something else is a better fit for your bedscape.
