Shadow welcomes unknown female bald eagle to his nest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026.
  • After the August death of Jackie, the female eagle he raised chicks with since 2018, Shadow began spending time with a 4-year-old female eagle named Kaydee (formerly KD1).
  • It has been revealed that cameras spotted the unknown female in the nest in recent weeks, but this was the first time the eagle was joined by Shadow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026. From suffering the loss of a clutch of eggs to welcoming two chicks, and from losing his longtime partner to finding a new friend, he’s had a tumultuous year.

After the August death of Jackie, the female eagle he raised chicks with since 2018, Shadow began spending time with a 4-year-old female eagle named Kaydee (formerly KD1). Viewers of the 24/7 livestream of Shadow’s nest could easily spot Kaydee because of her double-banded legs—a silver ring on one leg and a lavender one on the other. The pair appeared chummy as they spent more time together, sharing stick-arranging duties, singing, and exchanging beaky kisses. An unexpected twist arrived this week with the appearance of an unknown female bald eagle spotted in the nest with Shadow.

It has been revealed that cameras spotted the unknown female in the nest in recent weeks, but this was the first time the eagle was joined by Shadow. On Monday afternoon, Shadow landed in the nest rapidly followed by the unknown female. The unknown female fiddled the nest sticks while vocalizing and Shadow appeared unbothered by her presence. Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Big Bear Lake.

As this is nature, all we can do is sit back and see what unfolds. Mating season is approaching, so we have to wait and see if Shadow selects a newly introduced partner. Female eagles in Substantial Bear Valley typically lay their first clutch of eggs in January. Tune in to Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) livestreams to follow the southern California eagles anytime.

Industry observers note that kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

In a recent development, kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee right now has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Big Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

Recent findings suggest that in January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

In a recent development, on July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

Industry observers note that she was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center noted that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below six percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

In a recent development, A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Substantial Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

The 10 Best Fitness Trackers, Tested by Our Fitness and Tech Experts

📅 15 Mar 2024 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, NOT SURE WHAT fitness tracker is right for you?
  • It has been revealed that on the most basic level, the best fitness trackers offer GPS connectivity to help you stay on your training course and basic activity tracking.
  • Depending on what your health and fitness goals are (like losing weight, improving your sleep, or cutting time off your mile PR), the best fitness trackers can help you identify where your training is lacking, optimize your stress levels, improve your recovery time, and streamline your training sessions and daily wellness habits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, NOT SURE WHAT fitness tracker is right for you? You've come to the right place. We've been wearing and documenting fitness trackers as far back as 2015, when we reviewed the very first Apple Watch. We started cross-comparing fitness trackers as early as 2017, when we broke down the best fitness trackers for activities like strength training, running, hiking, golf, and more. Now in 2026, we're more dialed into the state of fitness trackers than ever before as nearly all our editors are wearing some sort of device on a daily basis.

It has been revealed that on the most basic level, the best fitness trackers offer GPS connectivity to help you stay on your training course and basic activity tracking. Newer iterations of fitness trackers include advanced smartwatches that can do anything from tracking your archery workout to detecting a heart attack, as well as (our personal favorite) smart rings. Smart rings pack a ton (no literally, an absurd amount) of sleep/stress stats and workout/health information into a tiny package you wear on your finger 24/7.

Depending on what your health and fitness goals are (like losing weight, improving your sleep, or cutting time off your mile PR), the best fitness trackers can help you identify where your training is lacking, optimize your stress levels, improve your recovery time, and streamline your training sessions and daily wellness habits.

According to recent reports, as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to test the latest and greatest fitness trackers. I am supported in this effort by my fellow editors like Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., Grooming Editor Sean Zucker, Senior Gear Editor Ryan Brower, and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. We have put countless fitness trackers through the gauntlet and evaluated models on accuracy, design, durability, and price. We also paid close attention to comfort, ease of use, syncing with our favorite apps, and their ability to meet our standards for any activity.

We revision our lineup of fitness trackers often, so you can expect up-to-date information that takes into account the latest fitness tracker releases.

According to recent reports, if you want a basic level fitness tracker, the Whoop PEAK membership with its new 5.0 band may be your answer. Men’s Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. backs this device for that reason. “Simplicity is what works here, because it's reliable, has great battery life, and I don't need to think about it,” he indicates. The Whoop 5.0 Band is a fitness tracker band, which means though it’s still decently functional, it does not have a display like most wrist devices. It tracks all of your data in the corresponding phone app, but it’s worth noting, you cannot see the data directly on your wrist.

Sources indicate that if you like the no-frills appearance, the Whoop 5.0 can definitely accomplish most of your tracking needs. “Whoop's activity sensing has improved over the years and continues to take steps,” claims Samuel. It can track anything from running, cycling, and rowing to weightlifting, yoga, soccer, and even massage therapy. From our personal experience with Whoop, we love how it fits on the wrist. It is one of the more comfortable fitness trackers we’ve worn—the strap has a soft back, is woven with microfilament yarn, and can also be easily adjusted.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, Samuel had some qualms with the heart rate monitoring. “The device isn't tremendously accurate in terms of tracking heart rate, which is important to note,” he says. “In general, note that whatever [Whoop] is telling you about heart rate, it's almost always overshooting.” This can be an problem because a lot of the other tracking metrics (calories, activity, etc.) are based around heart rate. However, if you just want something basic to wear on your wrist, count your steps, and give you a general look into your health and workouts, Whoop 5.0 Band with the Peak membership will do just that.

Industry observers note that read More: Garmin Vs. Apple Watch.

Oura was a pioneer in the smart ring space, and it’s still the best smart ring we’ve tested to date (and we’ve tested a lot). Multiple editors have been wearing an Oura Ring for the last ten years and can attest that each latest iteration outkicks the competition. This particular release updated a few physical features: Oura shifted to a fully titanium build (vs. a titanium exterior, epoxy interior), added smaller and larger sizes, and ditched its three-nodule sensor design. This latest model eliminates the nodules that used to be on the inside of the ring and pinch into my finger on the Oura Ring 3. Those aren't required anymore with the new tech, so that is a huge improvement over the past model.

It has been revealed that the battery can also last up to eight days now, instead of just seven. And the updated software is available on all models, upcoming and old. While Oura has always offered heart rate monitoring, the new software now features automatic heart rate monitoring, allowing you to detect and track your workout stats without hitting the “Record HR workout” button. This automatic detection feature also lends itself to workout monitoring for over 40 activities (a new capability compared to the past, solely cardio-focused tracking that Oura offered).

Industry observers note that the daytime stress features have also gotten an improvement—one of our favorites is illness detection. The Oura Ring 5 can detect changes in your stress stats and body temperature that may indicate an illness before you feel the entirety of the symptoms. A couple of months ago, one editor felt a slight earache when they woke up, and Oura called out they may have a cold coming on. The next day, that cold had arrived. It’s not always entirely accurate like this—there have been a few times the Oura Ring has noted we were getting sick when it was actually just a hangover (oops).

Even as Oura lovers, we’d be remiss not to call out one of the downsides to the product: In order to attain full use of the Oura Ring, you need to pay a monthly subscription fee of $5.99 (or $69.99 per year). There are other smart rings in the space that don’t require any fee (shout out to our second favorite product, the Ultrahuman ring), but with the updated technology and consistent top-of-the-line features, we deem the extra $69.99 per year a pretty minimal price to pay.

For the most style-conscious people, the firm also released a Ceramic version of the Oura Ring 4, which offers a unique look and additional color options.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Oura Ring 5.

Industry observers note that adventurers, look this way. We’re not exaggerating when we say this is the most rugged fitness tracker we have tested. The Garmin Instinct 3 AMOLED is packed with technology and has a thick face made for trail hikes, rock climbing, and even swimming (it’s water rated up to 100 meters). According to Men’s Health contributor Korin Miller, this Garmin can take a beating. “I accidentally banged it into several doorways and even scraped it against a kettlebell during a clumsy gym moment—it still looks brand fresh,” Miller states.

In a recent development, in addition to its outwardly masculine look and durable design, the technology here is super simple to navigate, which can’t be noted for all fitness trackers. Though there’s no touchscreen, Miller had the five buttons figured out within just a few minutes of receiving the product. And while you can track up to 30 different workout types, Miller praises the display for the easy-to-digest layout outside of workout mode. “The 390-by-390-pixel AMOLED display resolution is sharp and bright, allowing Garmin to jam a lot of stats on the home screen. At a glance, you can see your step count, heart rate, weather, date, time, and more. It’s arranged smartly in a way to deliver plenty of information without feeling overwhelming,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that but one of our favorite features? Garmin prioritizes a wind-down time, switching from a jam-packed interface to just a clock during the time you are typically sleeping (which you note during set-up). It’s worth mentioning that in order to be this rugged and durable, the Garmin Instinct 3 is also quite heavy at 53 grams. But if you’re going hard on the trails, there’s no better wrist partner.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Garmin Instinct 3.

Industry observers note that at this cost, you’d expect a simple appearance, no touchscreen, and limited functionality. However, the Google Pixel Watch 5 has a beautiful, easy-to-navigate touchscreen, a smooth design, and almost all the metrics you’d get on a more high-end device.

Google puts a substantial emphasis on overall wellness rather than just fitness tracking, focusing on breathing and stress management. “This is a very underrated device and it's gotten more accurate with the third edition,” says Samuel. “The breathing exercises don't reinvent the wheel, but the presentation is solid and the timing is good. Overall, in this market, there's a lot we don't fully understand about stress levels, and some of the algorithms are simplistic. But Google has smartly gotten us thinking about how we feel, and that's a good thing.”.

If this watch tracks stress, readiness, and sleep, what are the limitations of this budget-friendly device? Well, it doesn’t offer as many workout modes as most other fitness trackers, clocking in at just 41 options. You also have to charge it every day, and it’s only compatible with Android devices. But for such a clean, aesthetic appearance and great individual wellness metrics, we definitely consider this fitness tracker a steal.

Sources indicate that most fitness trackers carry a hefty price tag, so if you’re in the market but not looking to sell out on this particular accessory, the Suunto Race S is the best value you’ll find. With a high definition AMOLED touchscreen, over 95 sport modes, and a water rating up to 50m, the specs here are just as good as you’ll find on many high-end fitness trackers. The AMOLED display on this watch is fantastic for its compact design. And personally, I think the Suunto Race S is superior to the larger model.

In a recent development, A lot of fitness trackers in this price range (around $350) offer only more basic tracking, like steps and calories burned. That’s not the case here, there is more to this fitness watch than just a run tracker—there are workouts and other great fitness insights, like HRV, sleep monitoring, activity tracking and race pacing. Sure, it's not as powerful as a top-of-the-line Garmin, but it gets the job done and brings great value.

Recent findings suggest that let’s chat about some of those features. Sleep tracking is having a moment and the Suunto Race S can track your sleep duration, timing, deep sleep, light sleep, heart rate, REM and HRV from sleep. One downside here? Wearing a watch to bed isn’t for everyone. Another cool feature worth digging into is race pacing. If you’re training for an upcoming marathon (or just life), the Race Pacer can help keep you on track when the mid-long run rut strikes. Overall, this is a great budget-friendly find—just note that if you opt for the titanium version over the stainless steel version, that will hike the price up by $120 (which makes it not as budget-friendly).

Apple fans already know how great the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is. It features a large, durable aerospace-grade titanium body built for outdoor adventure. It’s water-rated up to 100m and boasts dual-frequency GPS. What’s that do for you exactly? It offers much more accurate tracking in tough environments (like densely populated cities, mountain terrain, and forests)—great for trail runners and climbers.

It has been revealed that apple has always been at the top of the game for fitness tracking. The Ultra 4 offers all the typical metrics of the older Apple Watch models—activity rings, over 60 workout modes, blood oxygen, ECG, etc. But the Ultra 4 can be used as a dive computer, an emergency siren, and a compass that retraces your steps (ideal for those prone to getting lost mid-hike).

Recent findings suggest that A watch that can do this much won’t look dainty on the wrist, though. Men’s Health Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM wrapped everything up nicely here. “The newly introduced design overhauled the sensor, which is on the rear of the watch and sits against the wearer’s wrist. Even though the casing is still the same 49-millimeter size as previous versions of the device and the sensor takes up the same amount of space.” Williams continues, “There’s now more surface area for device-to-skin contact for ECG readings, a new, circular optical sensing array, and larger, more efficient LEDs for heart rate sensing.”.

For us, the only real downside is that it’s a bit chunky on the wrist, but we’ll take it—the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is truly the full package for all iPhone users.

Read More: Our Hands-On Test of the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

If you’ve ever been big into running, you’ve likely considered a Garmin watch. But the Garmin Fēnix 9 isn’t just great for run tracking—it tracks over 100 different types of workouts and can last up to 29 days on one charge. In addition to its functionality, the Garmin Fēnix 9 also boasts a high-end design. One of the thinner offerings in the way of chunky Garmins, this is the perfect fitness tracking watch for anyone who doesn’t want to wear anything too cumbersome on the wrist (plus it now comes in a 43mm size). This watch has everything that fitness tracking powerhouse Garmin has to offer packed into its low-profile casing.

One of the coolest offerings? Garmin has both an AMOLED and a solar-powered option. The solar-powered watch can extend the battery life even further, but the screen is not quite as bright as the AMOLED option. The solar watch also does not have a touchscreen like the AMOLED one, making it a bit less convenient to have to click through the features via buttons.

In a recent development, while the Garmin Fēnix 9 has the capabilities to track pretty much any metric you want tracked, the charging experience falls a bit short. While the battery can last up to 24 days in low-power mode, turning on GPS drops that to just under 24 hours of charge—a stark difference. Additionally, the charging cord is a bit short, so you might want to keep these USB-C charger extension cords on hand to charge your Garmin.

It has been revealed that overall, this is a sleek, all-in-one package with a unique (and modern) solar-powered option. If you don’t mind a bit of a sub-par charging experience, you can’t get more premium than the Garmin Fēnix 9.

It has been revealed that no iPhone? No problem. The Galaxy Watch9 can go anywhere thanks to a large scratch-resistant screen and a strong titanium case. One of our favorite features is the advanced sleep coaching that analyzes your sleep habits, suggests what you can do to improve, and is even FDA-approved to detect sleep apnea. We also appreciate the body composition reader—in just a few seconds, the Galaxy Watch9 works to tell you your vitals, and even provides a body fat estimate. These stats are prone to inaccuracy (few home devices can accurately track body fat), but we give props to Samsung for trying to push metrics to another level.

Recent findings suggest that the Galaxy Watch9 also delivers the features you expect in high-end smartwatches. That means accurate dual-frequency GPS specs and voice navigation. Nailing these (as Samsung does) is extra-critical, partly because the Galaxy Watch9 has some latest competition for Android users (namely, from Google's Pixel Watch).

Thanks to several generations of trial and error and newly introduced AI health insights, the Galaxy Watch gets the edge as our preferred pick for Android owners. There are more health insights and data in this watch than most competitors. Once you grant the device access to your health insights on your phone, it will make recommendations on sleep, exercise, and overall health, after you choose what your own personal goals are. I appreciate the design as well, which looks more like a classic watch than other smartwatch options.

The array of features available and the materials used to craft the watch have been optimized a few times over, thus producing a seriously strong, long-lasting fitness tracker (and everyday smart watch) most customers will be happy adding to their training arsenal.

Read More: The Best Smartwatches.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re just starting out, you probably want a no-fuss fitness tracker to help get your bearings. The G-Shock Move is easy to navigate and offers just enough tracking to get you started. Men’s Health Grooming and Commerce Editor Sean Zucker tested it out for himself and likes how easy it is for newbies. “Thankfully, where the watch really excels is where it’s most meant to be used—when you’re working out or going for a run,” Zucker notes. “Its face has a simple design and navigating it was a breeze, even for someone as technologically challenged as myself. It was easy to switch between lap/route times, heart rate/zone, homepage, etc. while I was running with only a couple of clicks (the watch itself only has 4 buttons so I appreciate the simplified design).”.

The G-Shock Move tracks all your basic needs: steps, running, walking, heart rate, blood oxygen, and even sleep recovery. Zucker also found it quite comfortable. “[It’s a] super comfortable watch, and handles sweat/rain with ease,” he says. “It doesn’t move around at all or get greasy after a long run/workout.” Though he did have a couple qualms with the functionality.

Recent findings suggest that “Now, I’m not someone who likes to wear a watch, let alone a fitness watch, all of the time but I will if I have a few minutes or I’m planning out a run,” says Zucker. “I’ll check in on what I’ve done that week and unfortunately, the app doesn’t let you access any of that info unless your phone is currently connected, which is, in my professional opinion, quite annoying.” Another small downside, Zucker did mention he had a tough time with initial setup.

Sources indicate that “It’s crucial to note that I am generally 100 years old and grumpy about this type of stuff, [but] still, the set up on this watch was a bit of a pain,” states Zucker. “There were a lot of ads (this extends to the app itself after you start using as well, very muddy).” If you can get past the setup and are okay with only being able to check past stats when you’re connected to the phone app, this is a great beginner-friendly tracker offering all the basic functions you need to kick off your fitness tracking journey.

Sources indicate that fitbit is back, with a vengeance. The Fitbit Air is the brand’s smallest and lightest tracker ever, weighing just 12 grams and featuring a design 25 percent smaller than the discontinued Luxe. Setup is simple through the fresh Google Health app, and the Air’s tracking features, including 24/7 heart rate, HRV, skin temperature, and sleep, run seamlessly in the background, with automatic workout detection and a reliable seven-day battery life.

In a recent development, what truly elevates the experience is the integration of Google’s Health Coach AI, available through a Google Health Premium subscription, which is included for those who already have Google One. Food logging is a surprise standout—you can snap a picture of your meal, and the app accurately breaks down the macros. While the core tracking functions are available without a subscription, the real value comes from the Premium features like AI coaching, deeper analytics, and adaptive looks. But you don’t need the membership for the basic features.

In a recent development, some trade-offs to consider: The Air is screenless, so you can’t check notifications or your heart rate on the go, which may take some getting used to for smartwatch people. The default band can feel a bit stiff, and you charge it off-wrist. Still, the Fitbit Air is a compelling option for those who want minimalist, screenless health tracking without a hefty commitment.

At $99 with no required subscription, it’s an accessible entry point for anyone who wants comprehensive health data and a genuinely helpful AI coach, especially those seeking a distraction-free, streamlined alternative to full-featured smartwatches.

Read More: Our Full Review of the Google Fitbit Air.

In a recent development, fitness trackers started as mostly wrist devices—from step counters like the Fitbit to the original Apple Watch. Now, you can choose from an array of fitness tracking watches or smart rings, all of which track far more than just your fitness. While most of these devices offer similar capabilities, the design you choose—watch or ring—will depend on your own personal aesthetic.

It has been revealed that do you prefer the look of a fitness tracker watch? Do you find it more convenient to navigate all your stats on your wrist? Or do you like the look of a ring better and prefer the sleeker, more compact design? If so, are you also agreeable to the fact that you will need to visit your phone app to view all of your stats? Only you have the answers to these personal questions.

Industry observers note that fitness trackers don’t just track fitness anymore. Sure, your workouts are still a key part of what these devices do, but in addition they’re also tracking your sleep, heart rhythm patterns, blood oxygen levels, HRV, stress, and even caffeine consumption. Fitness trackers are more of an overall wellness tool than ever before.

That said, the type of fitness tracker you choose should weigh heavily on the way you intend to use it. If you’re just looking for insights into your sleep cycle, you’ll probably want a smart ring that’s fairly comfortable to wear to bed each night. If you’re training for a marathon, you may want a watch with a touchscreen that’s easy to navigate mid-run. This last part may be especially important: If you’re already using certain tracking apps that you love (let’s say, Apple Fitness for instance), you’ll want to make sure you find yourself a fitness tracker that is compatible with that app in particular.

According to recent reports, the accuracy of a fitness tracker begins and ends with how precisely it tracks your heart rate (most other stats, with the exception of new hydration tracking features, are derived from this baseline data). This mark is as much about pure accuracy as it is about consistency of accuracy, which is key in helping you understand your own fitness trends. While some trackers tend to be more accurate than others, all of the trackers we included here were consistently accurate.

With the exception of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Samsung Galaxy Watch9 (two fitness trackers that are equal parts smartwatch but have seen improvement in their battery life), the fitness trackers we tested are all designed to run for days (even weeks) on a single charge. We love a fitness tracker that needs minimal charging, and we also love a fitness tracker that can run for a long time when running its GPS mode. Two fitness trackers that surprised us when testing battery life include the Suunto Race S (up to 13 days on a single charge) and the Garmin Instinct 3 (21 days on a single charge when set to its most basic mode).

According to recent reports, all fitness trackers are made to take a beating, but some are better designed than others. Look at case construction, screen construction, and for smart rings, material. The most advanced fitness trackers (smart rings included) are typically made with stainless steel, titanium, or another type of quality metal. For screens, sapphire glass is a premium spec to look for thanks to its high scratch resistance and strength.

Sometimes the most durable fitness tracker is unnecessary, though, especially if you are using it for pavement running. In fact, a plastic construction fitness tracker can be a much better choice for cardio-intensive activities like running and biking, since the material is going to be much lighter than stainless steel or titanium. On the flip side, if you are using your fitness tracker for strength training (or hiking or trail running), it would make sense to look for stronger materials.

Latest Update: Why Sleep Consistency May Be the Missing Piece When It Comes to Heart Health

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing.
  • As it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that.
  • Recent findings suggest that before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some key context to understand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing. But what happens if you’re consistently hitting that goal while going to bed at different times? Think 10 p.m. on Monday, midnight on Wednesday, and well past 1 a.m. on Saturday because it’s the weekend, after all.

As it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that. New research suggests that sleep consistency—which includes both when you go to bed and wake up, and how much sleep you get from night to night—could play an notable role in cardiovascular health. And, while getting the recommended amount of shut-eye still matters, researchers are finding that how much your sleep fluctuates may deserve some attention, too.

Recent findings suggest that before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some key context to understand. Here's what the research actually found, why your body seems to care so much about routine, and how consistent your sleep schedule really needs to be.

Meet the experts: Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet, MD, PhD, is a neuroscientist and postdoctoral research fellow at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School and lead researcher of the upcoming study. Nour Makarem, PhD, is a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, is a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

For the latest study published in Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, researchers analyzed more than one million nights of sleep data from 10,362 adults participating in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program, an initiative that aims to collect data from over one million Americans and create the country’s largest biomedical database.

According to recent reports, unlike previous studies that only looked at people's sleep habits for about a week, this one used about six months of Fitbit data to see how participants' bedtimes, wake-up times, and total sleep duration changed from night to night. They then compared those patterns with participants’ medical records and tracked their health for nearly four years.

The findings were pretty eye-opening: For every additional 29 minutes of variation in how long someone slept from night to night, their relative risk of serious heart problems, including heart attacks, heart failure, heart muscle disease, and certain strokes, was 24 percent higher. To be clear, that doesn't mean going to bed 29 minutes later than usual on a given night increases your heart disease risk by 24 percent. The researchers were looking at a statistical measure of how much someone's total sleep duration varied over time, rather than the consequences of one late bedtime. As of now, all this information does it point to a potential link between sleep schedule variation and heart disease.

It has been revealed that researchers also found that greater night-to-night fluctuations in bedtime and wake-up times were associated with a 23 percent and 20 percent higher relative risk of cardiovascular problems, respectively. This means that both the consistency of your sleep schedule and the consistency of the duration of that sleep may play a role in heart health.

There are a few things worth keeping in mind, though. For starters, this study found a connection between inconsistent sleep and heart problems, but it couldn't prove that irregular sleep is what causes those problems. In fact, Viet points out that the relationship could work in the opposite direction too (i.e. early illness might actually make someone’s sleep more irregular). Plus, most participants were women and white, so we can't necessarily assume the findings apply to everyone. Still, the results add to growing evidence that sleep consistency deserves a place in the heart-health conversation.

Recent findings suggest that your body has its own internal clock, known as your circadian rhythm, which determines when you're tired, when you're wide awake, and even how bodily functions like blood pressure and heart rate change throughout the day. And, it works at its best when it has a reasonably predictable schedule to follow. When you're constantly changing when you sleep and wake, you may disrupt that rhythm, a phenomenon known as circadian misalignment, explains Nour Makarem, PhD, a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

That disruption can impact some pretty notable cardiovascular processes, like how your body regulates blood pressure. Under normal circumstances, blood pressure usually drops by about 10 to 20 percent while you're sleeping to give your cardiovascular system a period of rest, but research by Makarem suggests that irregular sleep patterns may be associated with higher blood pressure and an increased risk of hypertension. “This is problematic because higher nocturnal blood pressure and having a non-dipping profile (blood pressure that does not dip or dip enough during sleep) are associated with higher risk for heart disease and stroke, the leading causes of death in women,” she says.

Industry observers note that your sleep schedule may also interact with other daily rhythms, including when you eat and exercise. These behaviors help regulate biological clocks throughout your body, including those involved in metabolism, Makarem notes. When those clocks fall out of sync, processes like blood sugar regulation may be affected, too. In fact, research has linked irregular sleep patterns with poorer glucose regulation and a higher risk of metabolic challenges.

Research is still emerging, but scientists are noticing some important links between sleep consistency and heart health. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health followed more than 72,000 adults and found that people with irregular sleep patterns had a higher risk of major cardiovascular events, including heart attacks and strokes. Another study published in Sleep in 2024 analyzed sleep patterns in more than 60,000 adults and found that sleep regularity was a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration in that population.

Recent findings suggest that so, does this mean having a consistent bed and rising time matters more than getting eight hours? Not necessarily. "The evidence for sleep regularity is rather nascent relative to that for sleep duration," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. She explains that while several studies have made the connection between irregular sleep and poorer health outcomes, more research needs to be done to determine whether making someone's sleep schedule more consistent can actually lower their cardiovascular risk. And, we do have plenty of evidence that getting enough sleep has positive affects on just about every system in the body, from brain function to muscle recovery.

Overall, there are still things researchers are learning about sleep consistency and heart health, but it’s safe to start thinking of it as another piece of the puzzle, alongside getting enough hours and making sure those hours are restorative.

Here's the million-dollar question: Does protecting your heart mean going to bed at exactly 10:30 p.m. every single night, no exceptions? Thankfully, no.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, you’ve got some wiggle room. "In general, we would recommend that individuals try not to deviate by 60 min up or down from their average bedtime or sleep duration," says St-Onge, but the smaller the gap, the better.

In a recent development, think of that as a target, not a hard-and-fast rule. An occasional late night or weekend sleep-in isn’t a reason to panic. What matters more is establishing a reasonably consistent pattern over a period of time rather than expecting yourself to follow a perfect schedule every single night.

In a recent development, if you've had a particularly short night, St-Onge recommends trying to go to bed a little earlier and waking up a little later when your schedule allows, rather than trying to make up for all that lost sleep by sleeping in for hours. Most importantly, don't sweat it. "If one night is off, it's not all doom and gloom; you get right back on schedule the following night," says St-Onge.

Here are a few small changes experts recommend to improve your sleep routine without completely overhauling your lifestyle.

Before committing to being in bed every night by 9 p.m., consider what will actually make sense for your schedule. Earlier isn't automatically better. What's important is getting adequate sleep on a schedule that works with your body's natural rhythm and everyday responsibilities, explains St-Onge.

If your current bedtime is midnight but you'd ideally like to be asleep by 11, there's no need to make that change all at once. Makarem recommends gradually shifting your bedtime earlier by about 10 minutes each day until you reach your target. The idea is to give your body time to adjust rather than suddenly expecting yourself to fall asleep an hour earlier than usual.

It's tempting to stay up late on Friday and Saturday nights and make up for it by sleeping well into the morning, but even those brief changes can leave you feeling out of sync by the time Monday rolls around. If possible, St-Onge recommends keeping your weekend bedtimes within about an hour of your usual routine.

Industry observers note that if you wear an Apple Watch or Fitbit to bed, you know how easy it is to get caught up in the numbers. One morning you're celebrating a great sleep score, and the next you're wondering what went wrong because your tracker claims you barely got any deep sleep.

While these devices can be helpful for spotting patterns, the last thing you want is to start losing sleep over your sleep. Makarem recommends using trackers to keep tabs on your habits or remind you when it's time for bed, but only if they're actually helping. If checking your sleep stats is making you anxious, it's fine to ditch the data and simply pay attention to when you're going to bed and waking up.

And remember, you don't have to get your sleep schedule exactly right every single night to do something good for your heart. Small changes that you can actually stick with are worth more than chasing a perfect score. As Makarem puts it, "Progress is better than perfect.".

Breaking: Whale snot helps scientists sequence an entire genome

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, whale vomit can be turned into expensive perfume.
  • Whole genomes are crucial for animal conservation.
  • According to recent reports, to obtain genetic data from whales, marine biologists historically have had to conduct a skin biopsy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, whale vomit can be turned into expensive perfume. Whale carcasses will sink to the bottom and become marine life habitats. Whale pee nourishes the entire ocean. But how about whale snot? The microbes and other biological material emitted from their blowholes when the giant cetaceans breathe has helped scientists sequence an entire whale genome: Take that whale vomit. The findings are detailed in a study published today in the journal Molecular Ecology Resources.

Whole genomes are crucial for animal conservation. With genomic data, researchers can measure population health, to see how much genetic diversity and inbreeding is present. It can also help identify individual animals for monitoring, help determine an animal’s sex, and estimate the population’s size.

According to recent reports, to obtain genetic data from whales, marine biologists historically have had to conduct a skin biopsy. They’ll take a dart, stick it into the whale’s blubber, and take a small sample of the skin and blubber. However, during sampling, boats must get close to the whales, which can disturb them. In some locations and for some endangered species, getting close enough to take a biopsy isn’t permitted or possible.

In a recent development, that’s where whale snot—or blow—comes in. For this study, a team from Scotland’s University of St. Andrews, the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, the North Coast Cetacean Society, and Fisheries and Oceans Canada used several small drones off the coast of British Columbia. The drones were equipped with sterile petri dishes to collect the samples.

In a recent development, the team flew the drone through the exhaled breaths of one North pacific humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae kuzira) at a time, but still sampled several individual whales. The humpbacks generally took one to six breaths every time they surfaced—covering the drone and the dishes in whale snot.

According to recent reports, the team collected 58 blow samples from 26 individual humpback whales. They also took repeated samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across two years to match the genomes. They then cross-referenced the genomes collected from the whale blow with genomes sequenced from traditional blubber biopsies taken from the same animals.

In a recent development, to keep the DNA from mixing, the team targeted the whale most upwind in the pod, since the blow downwind might mix with the blow from the whales up ahead. Resting whales were never sampled, and the team stopped the drone flights if a whale indicated any reaction. More than one third of samples were collected by flying the drone directly from land—no boat required.

The DNA was sequenced to produce two types of genomes. Low-coverage nuclear genomes, which are inherited from both parents, and high-coverage mitochondrial genomes, which are inherited from the mother only.

The team found that the genetic diversity estimated from the blow samples was very similar to the estimates taken from traditional biopsies. Fortunately, the humpback population in the study reveals little evidence of recent inbreeding. There is a small proportion of the genome that has long stretches of identical DNA, but the team believes that most likely reflects distant shared ancestry or past population bottlenecks.

According to the team, this research marks one of the first whole genome datasets for a group of North Pacific humpback whales. Previously, only one North Pacific humpback whole genome was publicly available.

In a recent development, “We will use these blow-derived genomes to not only assess population structure and health, but also assess kinship and family ties among humpback whales foraging in northern British Columbia,” Dr. Éadin O’Mahony, a study co-author and marine mammal ecologist who was at the University of St. Andrews at the time of the study, remarked in a statement. “The aim is to understand how their social bonds form: Are the whales that forage together family, or long-term friends?”.

Industry observers note that as expected, the North Pacific humpback whales were genetically distinct from their counterparts living in the North Atlantic. This confirms that data taken from whale blow works as well from data taken from conventional biopsies. The drone-captured genetic analyses also correctly determined every whale’s sex, and revealed three previously undescribed mitochondrial DNA variants, which could help show how some of these whales are related. The blow from whales swimming in groups also did not have any sign of contamination from neighboring whales.

According to recent reports, about 16 percent of the DNA in each blow sample were also primarily from the microbes living in the whale’s airways. According to the team, this indicates that a single breath could tell us about the individual whale and its respiratory microbiome, opening up a potential fresh window into cetacean health.

That’s a whole lot of data from just a little bit of snot.

A Minimalist House in Italy Makes the Case for Less

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in Latest York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein.
  • Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint.
  • Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The friendship between John Pawson and Noona Smith-Petersen began in Latest York City in a very 1990s way: working for Calvin Klein. Pawson, then an architectural wunderkind from the United Kingdom, and Smith-Petersen, a young Danish-Italian communications manager for the fashion house, found themselves collaborating on the opening of the brand’s first flagship on Madison Avenue.

Pawson had already earned a reputation for restraint. His earliest residential works (a Mallorca summer house for collectors, an art dealer’s London apartment) provided a series of simple surfaces, plinths, and frames—for objects, for vistas, and for life. The same was true at the Calvin Klein store, where designer and client amplified each other’s design approaches in a meeting of minimalist minds.

Furnished with Hans Wegner chairs and a Pawson-designed table, the dining area opens onto the land thanks to a sliding window wall.

The living area features a table and chairs by Poul Kjærholm.

A sauna is clad in blackened wood.

Sources indicate that pawson’s recent residence for Smith-Petersen and her husband, Enrico Erba Springorum, an Armani executive, makes another case for life with less. “The imprint came from childhood: the minimalism, the Danish design,” explains Smith-Petersen, who grew up outside Copenhagen. “Poul Kjærholm was our neighbor,” she adds, name-checking the widely influential midcentury modernist. There were also formative summers spent at the pared-back house her father designed on the Turkish peninsula of Çeşme. About the location, she recalls, “People noted, ‘You guys are crazy!’ But it was a place close to nature and the sea. And then later it became a destination.”.

A single sculptural tree dots the courtyard.

An oak bed with integrated bedside tables anchors the primary bedroom.

Ninety minutes south of Milan, the patchwork hills of the Val Luretta are far less isolated. Its proximity to the city has attracted editors, artists, and other creatives in search of space and quiet. That tranquility drew Smith-Petersen to the area when she was seeking land on which to build a compound with her younger brother, Henrik, for their families. (She and her husband have two adult sons.) Over the years, she and Pawson had maintained a friendship. “So when Henrik and I found the property, I had this crazy idea: Why don’t I ask John?” says Smith-Petersen. “My brother remarked, ‘Forget it!’ But we went to visit John and his team in London and it kicked off from there.”.

The primary bath’s bespoke vanity, topped in a Grassi Pietri surface.

Smith-Petersen stands in the living area.

A view across the dining table toward the minimalist hearth.

The resulting structure, realized with project architect Giulio Marchesi, is the irst of two planned homes on the site, one for each sibling. Sitting long and low on the land, like an ivory piano key dropped onto the hillside, the single-story house frames expansive views of the Val Luretta. “The area of the countryside is so dramatic,” reflects Pawson, whose first visit to the site was in winter fog. “In the summer, it’s very different—it’s so lush.”.

It has been revealed that at some 2,500 square feet, the house is spacious but intimate, with Pawson’s trademark spareness and remarkable warmth. He designed it along one axis, a long corridor connecting the foyer to the open-blueprint kitchen, dining area, and living area, then bedrooms beyond. White-painted plaster walls and floors of pale-gray stone, sourced nearby in Vicenza, radiate calm. As Pawson explains, understanding the way the body and the eye move through a space is paramount—and can take time. “You’ve got to learn the choreography,” he states. Living in and feeling the house is key.

Smith-Petersen and Pawson on-site.

The yearslong friendship Pawson and Smith-Petersen had forged helped him understand how she would use the space. There would be mornings at the Pawson-designed table, afternoons on the terrace or under one of the century-old oaks, and evenings making dinner in a kitchen brimming with Scandinavian tableware. In solitude or surrounded by family, there’s complete peace on offer.

The open-plan dining area and kitchen.

“Most architects—contemporaries, colleagues—always say, ‘Oh, it’s impossible, a private house,’ ” says Pawson. The process can be “very emotional. And that’s what makes it good.” Luckily for Smith-Petersen, the primary feeling the house evokes is serenity. “I didn’t expect to be in such awe,” she says. “I was never a country person. Sometimes, I try to arrive a day before anyone else is here and do a silent retreat,” she adds. “It’s where I feel best now. It’s pure joy.”.

Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Notes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.
  • In a recent development, the updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year.
  • The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

In a recent development, the updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

According to recent reports, the new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

Recent findings suggest that these findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), mentioned in a statement.

In a recent development, the CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:.

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”.

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he mentioned.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”.

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” stated Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Recent findings suggest that cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

It has been revealed that candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

Sources indicate that while those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:.

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:.

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is right now under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

Coffee could have anti-aging benefits. Here’s why.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.
  • According to recent reports, the one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee.
  • Sources indicate that despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a handful of foods and beverages—red wine, eggs, and cooking oils—whose reputations tend to pendulum-swing routinely between “lifesaving” and “death sentence.” I usually hedge my bets by eating these confusing foods in moderation.

According to recent reports, the one item I have trouble consuming in moderation might be the most contentious of all: coffee. I am so hopelessly addicted to the stuff that I usually need at least one cup of coffee before going out to meet a friend for coffee.

Sources indicate that despite my unwavering devotion to coffee, the jury is still out on whether my daily fix is actually good for my health. Throughout my lifetime, coffee has variously been purported to protect my heart, disrupt its rhythm, reduce my risk of cancer, and increase it. All I know is it helps me become a fully conscious person every morning. But could my coffee habit actually reduce wrinkles and help me age more gracefully?

A new study conducted at Texas A&M suggests that certain compounds in coffee might protect the body against aging and inflammation.

However, according to Dr. Dung Trinh, the chief medical officer at Healthy Brain Clinic in Long Beach, California, it’s probably too soon to pop open the champagne (or brew a celebratory pot) over the potential perks of your coffee habit.

“It’s far too early to treat coffee—or caffeic acid—as an anti-aging intervention,” Trinh tells Popular Science.

Sources indicate that despite its inconsistent status as a health food, coffee has been consistently linked to longer life and a lower likelihood of certain diseases, though it’s not certain why. The Texas A&M study, led by Dr. Stephen Safe, focused on a cellular receptor called NR4A1.

NR4A1 is a protein that regulates how cells respond to stress and damage. The study found that several compounds in coffee, particularly polyphenols—plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties—bind to the NR4A1 receptor. One of these polyphenols, caffeic acid, is found in coffee and many other plants and, despite its name, has nothing to do with caffeine. These compounds seem to promote NR4A1’s protective effects, including mitigating cellular damage and slowing the growth of cancer cell line in laboratory models.

According to recent reports, in other words, the harder your NR4A1 proteins are working, the better your cells may be at fending off damage. Sign me up!

According to recent reports, after researchers removed NR4A1 from cells in the lab, those benefits stopped, suggesting this receptor may help produce them. So, if coffee really helps NR4A1 do its job, we might just have a new anti-aging drink on our hands.

Interestingly, caffeine does not appear to play a key part in this mechanism, Trinh states. Instead, those benefits seem to come from coffee’s other compounds, like caffeic acid and its fellow polyphenols.

“What stood out to me was that the story was not really about caffeine,” he indicates. “I also found it interesting that the researchers did more than simply show that these compounds could bind to the receptor—they demonstrated NR4A1-dependent effects in cells. That makes the mechanism more compelling.”.

Translation: The study didn’t just show that coffee compounds attach to NR4A1; it revealed that this binding actually seems to activate the protein’s protective effects.

Consistent with this, the study also found that decaf coffee demonstrated similar protective effects on the lab cells, providing further evidence that coffee’s benefits may not have anything to do with caffeine at all.

It has been revealed that “One of the interesting messages from this paper is that coffee should not be thought of as simply a delivery system for caffeine,” Trinh says. “Caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, ferulic acid, and several other coffee compounds all interacted with NR4A1, while caffeine showed much more variable NR4A1-related activity.”.

So, coffee’s superpower might not come from caffeine at all, at least when it comes to anti-aging benefits.

Before you start guzzling triple lattes in the name of cellular protection, know that “more” does not always mean “better.”.

According to recent reports, “We simply cannot infer from this study that more coffee means more NR4A1 benefit,” Trinh states. This is because the researchers studied coffee extracts and purified compounds in a lab setting rather than giving human subjects increasing amounts of coffee and measuring NR4A1 activity. Plus, in human biology, it’s possible to have too much of a good thing, Trinh says.

“At some point, additional coffee can bring unwanted effects from caffeine, including sleep disruption, anxiety, palpitations, or increases in blood pressure in susceptible people,” he says. “Those effects could counteract other health benefits. So, this study should not be interpreted as establishing either an optimal number of cups or a dose-response relationship for this pathway.”.

Trinh adds that as compelling as the study’s findings are, he doesn’t yet believe they justify changing recommendations around coffee consumption.

Earlier studies have linked coffee drinking to living longer and to better outcomes for some age-related conditions, Trinh claims. But those studies couldn’t explain why. This one offers “one possible biological explanation,” he says.

Like most early-stage research, Trinh says, this study can’t be applied to humans sipping their morning “cup of ambition.” Much of the work used a specific cancer cell in the lab, along with mouse immune cells, rather than testing regular human coffee drinkers directly. And while the study identified a potentially promising mechanism, it’s not clear how this mechanism will translate to human health outcomes.

Ultimately, Trinh notes, no single food or compound is likely to be the deciding factor in how well we age.

For a coffee addict like myself, though, these findings are the best kind of wake-up call. Coffee may or may not turn back the clock, but it does stop me from hitting snooze 15 times.

“The much bigger determinants of healthy aging remain things such as regular physical activity, good sleep, avoiding smoking, controlling blood pressure and metabolic risk, maintaining social and cognitive engagement, and eating an overall nutritious diet,” Trinh indicates.

“This study is a promising piece of the scientific puzzle, not a prescription for another cup of coffee.”.

Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi indicates this tech alone is why this shoe is an absolute workhorse when it comes to running (and running fast!). The toebox has a ton of room for movement, but still holds the foot in place so each step feels responsive and energetic. On’s innovative speedboard, a flexible plastic plate wedged between the footbed and midsole, snaps back into place for a bouncy effect after your feet hit the ground. This means the shoe requires less energy output with each stride, making running feel easier. Plus, the rebound that comes with the underfoot cushioning gives a spring in your step.

According to recent reports, I might not run marathons like Accardi, but I love to wear this shoe for walking and casual jogs. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that THERE COMES A time in every man’s life—sans the few genetically gifted—when he must face hair loss. It hits sooner than many expect, as the American Hair Loss Association notes that 85 percent of men will face hair loss by age 50. There are then two options: lean into it and join the Stanley Tucci Gang, or invest in equipment to regrow hair. For the latter, the best tools to reverse balding at home are laser hair growth devices.

The majority of men lose their hair due to male pattern baldness (also known as androgenetic alopecia), a condition caused by genetic predisposition and hormonal influences, wherein testosterone is declining and dihydrotestosterone (aka DHT) is surging. This process is characterized by the classic receding hairline look, along with thinning around the crown.

In a recent development, laser hair growth devices are best at treating this cause of hair loss, explains dermatologist and founder of Remedy, Dr. Muneeb Shah, MD. Other common factors like stress, illness, medications, nutritional deficiencies, and autoimmune diseases will be less responsive to laser therapies, as hair follicles are often damaged or inactive from these issues and less willing to be rebooted from light treatment.

Laser hair growth devices work by using low-level laser therapy, or LLLT, to stimulate weakened or dormant hair follicles, claims hair restoration physician and creator of the Bauman Turbo LaserCap, Dr. Alan Bauman, MD. The process is known as photobiomodulation, and it involves exposing tissues to light in the red and near-infrared spectrum, which can improve cell metabolism and blood flow, reduce inflammation, and stimulate hair follicles to re-enter and maintain the growth phase.

According to recent reports, generally, LLLT does not include LED; instead, it uses laser diodes. However, some devices will combine both for added effectiveness or to reduce the intensity of laser diodes. “In simpler terms, laser therapy supercharges the environment for healthy hair growth by restoring energy to sluggish follicles and optimizing scalp conditions,” Dr. Bauman says.

Laser hair growth devices are rarely cheap (you won’t find an effective one below $400), so you want to make sure you’re getting the right option for you before making the investment. After chatting with the pros, these are the five laser hair growth devices worth considering.

The biggest dilemma when buying a laser hair growth device is choosing between LED and laser diodes, but with the iRestore Laser Therapy Hair Growth System, you don’t have to. This device uses a hybrid of laser diodes and LEDs to get the best of both worlds, pairing the gentle nature of LEDs with the power of laser diodes. Dr. Shah backs it, noting that iRestore is reputable and the device is FDA-cleared.

The brand even offers a six-month money-back guarantee if no results are seen. However, I’d imagine the brand doesn’t receive many sendbacks, as this device gives full coverage with serious results. According to recent reports, dr. Shah also recommends this offering from Current Body. This futuristic helmet offers a spectrum of red light LED from 620 to 660 nanometers. The flexible intensity allows for a customized experience, which is ideal for those new to these tools or with sensitive skin to ease into LED treatment and see what your ideal nanometer level is.

While results will be stronger closer to 650 or 660 nanometers, this range is powerful enough to reduce inflammation, decrease DHT levels (to maintain follicle strength), and improve blood flow on the scalp (to provide hair follicles with more oxygen and nutrients needed for growth).

Sure, it may look like a VR set from a scrapped Black Mirror episode, but it’s quite comfortable, and deceptively adjustable for a quality fit. Use for 10 minutes daily, and results can be seen quickly in as little as 16 weeks. Not everybody has the budget (or desire) to drop several thousand on a hair growth device. Maybe you’re on the fence about these tools, or the prospect of regrowing your hair in general. For these folks, Hairmax will be your best option, as it’s the least expensive tool on the market that’s still effective.

Featuring 12 medical-grade laser diodes in a comb-style tool, you gently brush this device through your hair and across your dome to stimulate hair growth. The sessions are listed at eight minutes; however, it often takes longer for the best results, given the manual nature of the device and the smaller surface it covers at once. Still, you won’t find a cheaper FDA-approved model.

Industry observers note that as Dr. Bauman puts it, not all laser hair growth devices are created equal. The first thing to consider is what light is being used in your device to stimulate growth. The two primary options are LEDs (Light Emitting Diodes) and laser diodes. He recommends zeroing in on laser diodes as they’re more powerful and penetrate deeper into the scalp, targeting the hair follicle root more effectively.

From a strict regrowth perspective, laser diodes will be more effective; however, these also present more potential side effects given their strength, such as hyperpigmentation, burns, redness, and swelling. LEDs present fewer side effects, so they’re better for sensitive scalps, but they won’t penetrate the scalp and hair follicles as deeply. This means LED is best suited for early shedding and will struggle to help more severe hair loss.

For both LED and laser diode options, the therapeutic wavelength is crucial. Dr. Shah recommends wavelengths between 630 and 680 nanometers to successfully penetrate the scalp and stimulate hair follicle growth. If you have sensitive skin or are fresh to these tools, take it slow and work your way to the top level to limit irritation.

Dr. Bauman says that the 650-nanometer range is key, as it is the optimal wavelength absorbed by mitochondria for energy production to support hair follicle function. This process boosts cellular energy, as hair follicles are highly active structures that need a lot of energy to support the hair growth cycle. The end result is reduced inflammation, improved blood flow, and extended growth.

In a recent development, to be clear, no laser hair growth device is going to give you Thor-level flow overnight—these tools take time. Dr. Shah claims that men will need at least six months of consistent use before seeing results after regular use. But not every device’s session will be the same. Some, you’ll need to wear or place near the dome for five minutes, while others for half an hour. Consider the comfort of your device, along with your schedule, before investing.

Most importantly, however, Dr. Shah states consistency is crucial because missing sessions, no matter how long they are, can reduce the device’s effectiveness. If executed properly, early results will appear around six months, such as reduced shedding or slight thickening, before fuller regrowth occurs near the one-year mark, according to Dr. Shah.

According to recent reports, whenever you’re dealing with upcoming technology, rely on reputable organizations to first approve it for use. Both Dr. Shah and Dr. Bauman advise only looking to laser hair growth devices that have been accepted by the FDA for the safest, most effective experience. However, there are different levels of FDA acceptance. FDA-listed or FDA-registered simply means that the manufacturer has informed the FDA, but doesn’t imply approval or authorization.

FDA clearance, on the other hand, means the device is substantially equivalent to a product already on the market.

FDA approved is the ideal, as this means the device has successfully been through extensive testing and clinical trials to demonstrate safety and effectiveness. But to date, there have been no LED or laser diode devices for hair growth that are FDA-approved, so look for FDA-cleared options.
