  • With Thanksgiving approaching, many of us are busy planning our menus.
  • While we may spend countless hours and enormous effort preparing the perfect meal, how much time do we invest in cultivating the emotion at the heart of the holiday?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

With Thanksgiving approaching, many of us are busy planning our menus. Turkey or ham? Mashed or roast potatoes? Pumpkin or pecan pie?

While we may spend countless hours and enormous effort preparing the perfect meal, how much time do we invest in cultivating the emotion at the heart of the holiday?

In a recent development, too often, gratitude is served up as a side dish—a brief expression of thanks before we dive into our feast. But what if we made gratitude the main course?

Gratitude offers enormous benefits for our physical and mental health. Given its importance, we dedicate an entire chapter to it in our book, Happy Together: Using the Science of Positive Psychology to Build Love That Lasts, and have written about it here, here, and here.

According to positive psychology research, it is one of the five most key character strengths for individual well-being. Leading emotion scientist Barbara Fredrickson similarly argues that it’s vital to our relationships, noting that couples who express gratitude well have a greater chance of staying together.

Recent research suggests that gratitude’s positive reach extends far beyond the two people directly involved.

In a recent development, in a paper published in Affective Science, researchers conducted two studies involving 680 participants. In the first study, participants watched a video of someone helping another person solve a problem. Afterward, the person who received help responded with either gratitude or simple positivity. Viewers then shared their personal impressions of that person. In the second study, participants had to decide whether to cooperate with the grateful person to earn money, even though doing so left them vulnerable to exploitation.

The researchers found that simply witnessing expressions of gratitude—rather than general positivity—fostered more favorable impressions of that person. In fact, it created a “halo effect” wherein participants felt greater trust, closeness, and willingness to interact with the grateful person, even when cooperating on a risky financial task. When people witness gratitude in action, it signals warmth and trustworthiness, creating opportunities to bring groups and communities together.

To build that same sense of trust, closeness, and community around your Thanksgiving table, try shifting how you share thanks this year.

This Thanksgiving, rather than just filling our plates, let’s also remember to focus on nourishing our relationships. Gratitude, it turns out, is a dish best shared—and its benefits may extend far beyond the people at the table.

I Went to Gee’s Bend to See Its Famous Quilts. Nothing Prepared Me for the Beauty

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares.
  • Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line. Over my shoulder, Doris Pettway Mosely watches my hands with the patience of someone who has been quilting since she was 11. She gently corrects my angle and sewing style, while Mary Margaret Pettway does the same for the rest of our small class. We laugh through most of it. Then Doris looks over my work and tells me my stitches are nice and short, and I sit up a little straighter.

Recent findings suggest that I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares. Mary Margaret, a fourth-generation quilter, has shown her work in major museums across the country. Doris, the daughter of celebrated quilter Leola Pettway, still sews her mother’s signature Z pattern alongside her own vivid, scrap-pieced designs. “I learned at four years old,” Mary Margaret tells me, explaining that she picked up the craft from her mother, Lucy T. Pettway. In their house, quilting was a chore like mopping or sweeping the yard, and the boys learned too.

Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

It has been revealed that after class, I wander the festival grounds, where quilts hang from clotheslines strung between wooden posts. A quilt of nested squares in navy and sky blue hangs next to one in butter yellow, punched with blocks of chartreuse and red. Another glows neon coral. Farther down the line, rings of pale pink, olive green, and rose-print fabric radiate out from a single center square, a take on the classic Housetop pattern. Inside the River Gallery, a quilt called Remembering Dinah is pieced from faded denim and mustard corduroy, its back pockets and frayed knees left intact. It’s a reminder of where this tradition began.

Children learning to quilt in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, in 2010.

Today, Gee’s Bend quilts hang in more than 40 museums, but they began as something far more practical. This small town takes its name from Joseph Gee, who established a cotton plantation in this bend of the Alabama River in 1816. Enslaved people and generations of their descendants stitched quilts to keep their families warm during winter and to brighten their homes, piecing them together from worn-out work clothes, denim, and whatever fabric scraps they had. Each year as summer gave way to fall, women hung their quilts outside to air before the cold set in, a tradition that inspired the Airing of the Quilts Festival, released in 2022 by nonprofit organizations Freedom Quilting Bee Legacy and Sew Gee’s Bend Heritage Builders.

A quilt on display in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

Among the community’s earliest known named quilters was Dinah Miller, who was taken from West Africa as a girl in 1860, likely aboard the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to reach the US. She settled in Gee’s Bend in the 1890s and passed her craft down. During the civil rights movement, the quilts became a financial lifeline. Black residents who tried to register to vote risked losing their jobs and the land they lived on to white landowners. In 1962, officials shut down the ferry connecting the community to the county seat, making it difficult to register to vote, and cutting them off from grocery stores, banks, schools, and medical care. The ferry didn’t run again until 2006.

In a recent development, four years after the closure, the community established the Freedom Quilting Bee, a cooperative that gave local women an income their white employers couldn’t take away. When Father Francis X. Walter, an Episcopal priest and Mobile native, saw the bold quilts on a trip to Wilcox County, he helped organize auctions in New York, where the striking designs caught the attention of tastemakers like Sister Parish. The quilts went on to sell at Bloomingdale’s and Saks Fifth Avenue.

“The Quilts of Gee's Bend” exhibit at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, in 2004.

In a recent development, the art world caught up decades later, when a landmark exhibition, “The Quilts of Gee’s Bend,” opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, in 2002, introducing the quilters to audiences far beyond Alabama. Today, their work is celebrated for its bold colors, inventive patterns, and astonishing craftsmanship. In 2006, 10 of the quilts appeared on US postage stamps. And this summer, Ralph Lauren debuted a limited-edition collection of apparel, quilts, and home goods featuring designs by quilters Claudia Pettway Charley and Loretta Pettway Bennett.

But for design lovers, the festival offers something no museum can: the chance to see the quilts in the place they were made, and to meet the individual women who made them. They’re still sewn by hand, too. “[An authentic] Gee’s Bend quilt is not quilted by a sewing machine,” Mary Margaret says. “And it’s important to understand that every quilt is not alike. Everyone who quilts is not alike.”.

In a recent development, our quilting class ends the way it began, with plenty of laughter as we tie off our last stitches. Everyone wants a photo with Doris and Mary Margaret, and a few students have even brought books featuring the quilters’ work to be signed.

Outside, the festival is in full swing, with more than 40 booths devoted to quilters selling their quilts and wall hangings, along with puzzles and notebooks printed with Gee’s Bend patterns, doormats, quilted totes, and pot holders.

Last year’s festival drew more than 2,500 people and over $870,000 in visitor spending for the state, and Mary Margaret says guests come from as far as France and England. “They want to immerse themselves in Gee’s Bend,” she says. Doris looks forward to it all year. “I get to meet a lot of people I’ve never seen before,” she says. This year, she was especially excited to meet a 97-year-old quilter from Marion, Alabama, whose work she admires.

Quilts hanging outside at the festival.

I’ve visited plenty of places where Black history is told in the past tense, on plaques and behind glass. Gee’s Bend feels different. Here, the history is alive, and the people who inherited it are setting the terms. That hasn’t always been easy. Over the years, indicates Mary Margaret, quilters have seen their work copied and sold without receiving compensation. The festival allows the public to buy directly from the quilters, at their booths or even from their porches, and know that the money is going straight to the artists.

Recent findings suggest that mostly, my day with the women of Gee’s Bend feels like a family reunion. The experience takes me straight back to childhood afternoons with my grandmother, who taught me to mend holes in pockets, sew patches onto my jeans jacket, and replace a button before anyone noticed it was missing.

It has been revealed that mary Margaret started even younger than I did, and now her own son and daughter are quilters themselves, working with patterns passed down through generations of the family. “To me a quilt states home,” says Mary Margaret. “It says warmth. It says care. It says time.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

According to recent reports, “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Manufacturer, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

It has been revealed that alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Sources indicate that currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A tiny, four-limbed soft robot resembling the cross between an octopus and an earthworm does more than inch across difficult terrain. With a process known as mechanoluminescence, the device glows as it moves and stretches without the need for external batteries or electronics. It’s not flimsy, either. Writing in a study recently published in the journal Small Structures, the soft robot’s inventors explained their design maintains its illuminating abilities after more than 1,000 stretching cycles.

Sources indicate that at South Korea’s Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST), engineer and study co-author Soon Moon Jeong believes the underlying dynamics at play are a promising newly introduced way to analyze and pinpoint deformations in a soft robot. It’s also potentially even more effective than existing softer options, since it doesn’t require additional components that might otherwise restrict the device’s movement.

Jeong’s team first designed a thin but resilient “tubular mechanoluminescent fiber” made from glowing particles of zinc sulfide and flexible polymers. They then filled elastic silicone tubes with the mixture, and wove them together into a mesh-like case for their pneumatic soft robot model. As the robot’s limbs stretch and contract, the zinc sulfide-infused polymer filling glows bright green specifically in the areas undergoing stress. Laboratory testing indicated their novel fibers withstood being pulled over twice their original length, and kept glowing after over 1,000 exercises.

Recent findings suggest that jeong noted his team is now focusing on improving the robot’s light emissions and resiliency. If successful, their mechanoluminescent fibers may be used in wearable medical devices or even artificial skins.

“The woven fiber-network configuration provides qualitative visual indication of deformation over the robotic body, offering a simple strategy for realizing self-visualizing soft robotic systems,” wrote the study’s authors, adding that their invention showcases the potential foundations for “next-generation self-visualizing intelligent soft systems.”.

This kettlebell is well-designed, stacking five weights in one relatively compact design. (Weight ranges include 8 to 16 kilograms, 16 to 24 kilograms, and 20 to 40 pounds.) To adjust the weight, just push down on the dial with two fingers, twist to your desired weight, and lift. It has a rubber base to protect your floors although—heads up—the rubber coating is only there when you use the kettlebell’s full weight. Otherwise, you’ll want to set down your kettlebell gingerly.

REP’s adjustable kettlebell is made from cast iron and feels durable. The textured handle is easy to grip and has plenty of space for two-handed moves, although it feels slightly wider than others. If space is a premium at your place and you’re looking to grow with your kettlebell, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment.

If you prefer a more traditional competition-style kettlebell, keep scrolling. But if you’re on the hunt for a highly versatile weight that aims to combine the attributes of a kettlebell with those of a dumbbell and a dual-grip medicine ball, the YBell Neo Series is worth consideration.

It has been revealed that this weight is perfect for my needs—it’s relatively compact and offers multiple ways to grip, thanks to its unique pyramid-style design. I can use it for everything from biceps curls to lunges, though it’s not ideal for swings.

The grip on this is perfection. It features a neoprene outer layer to create a slightly sticky feel with impressive gripping power, so I’m not stressed about accidentally flinging it across the room during swings. The wide handle leaves enough room for one- or two-handed exercises, but it may feel a little crowded using both mitts at once if your hands are on the larger side.

You have three different spots you can grip on the outside of this weight, along with an inside bar that’s ideal for dumbbell-style work. While the sides are rounded, I found it was relatively easy to rest the YBell on its base or sides to save space.

In a recent development, the only potential downside of this weight is that it tops out at 26 pounds. If you’re interested in doing heavier lifting, you’ll need to upgrade to a different device.

Recent findings suggest that A coated kettlebell like this one from Yes4All protects your floors in case of butterfingers through a thoughtfully wrapped coating up the bottom third of the handle. The handle itself makes for a comfortable grip. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi claims, “I have the 15-pound model and I never feel it slipping away from me when squatting or doing Russian twists.” It comes in five-pound increments up to 65 pounds, giving you plenty of options.

Recent findings suggest that while I wouldn’t recommend tossing this on your floor at home, the kettlebell doesn’t make a loud noise when it’s dropped, unlike uncoated models. It’s also worth pointing out it’s very affordable, similar to our best overall.Just note the bottom of the kettlebell is not entirely flat, which can be tricky if you’re trying exercises like uneven pushups (with one hand placed through the handles of a KB).

Sources indicate that sand kettlebells are a highly portable option that allows you to add a little more instability to your kettlebell workouts. The GoRuck Sand Kettlebell is built tough thanks to its Cordura nylon design and multiple closure system, so you don’t have to stress about accidentally spilling its contents all over the place.

GoRuck’s kettlebell has a teardrop-style shape that works well for many exercises. This kettlebell arrives empty, so you’ll fill it up with sand prior to use. Pro tip: use playground sand available at home improvement stores for this. The reinforcing on nearly all of the seams and bottoms means you can toss this on the ground without worrying about it flying open and spilling sand everywhere.

This style of kettlebell isn’t for everyone, but if you’re looking to add the extra challenge of sandbag training to your kettlebell workouts, this sand kettlebell design will take a lot of abuse and holds up well over time.

“When choosing the correct weight for your kettlebell, it is important to consider your exercise,” says Almoni Ellis, CSCS, CPT. She says that people generally are able to use heavier weights when doing purely lower-body exercises, but that those weights may be too heavy for a person when they’re doing a move like an overhead press, for example.

That said, there’s no one-size-fits-all starting point. Your experience level and current strength come into play, so if you’re unsure where to begin, try testing different weights at a local gym or consider ordering two sizes to see what feels best. As your strength improves, you can gradually increase the weight, adds Pack.

Sources indicate that the most common option for general strength training is the cast-iron kettlebell, which works well for everything from goblet squats to cleans to swings. These are the kettlebells you’ll most often see in home gyms and fitness classes.

Recent findings suggest that ellis and Pack recommend choosing a cast iron or steel kettlebell because they’re the most durable and long-lasting materials. “Kettlebells [that are] made up of plastic[...] don’t last as long,” Pack indicates.

Industry observers note that however, most adjustable kettlebells are made with some plastic components, which is necessary for the design. As for vinyl-coated kettlebells, they’re usually made of cast iron with a vinyl coating to prevent damage to floors.

Handle thickness plays a role in both comfort and performance. “Thicker handles can help build grip strength, but they may be more challenging for beginners to control,” says Pack.

The handle’s coating and texture matter just as much. A slightly textured surface can help you maintain a secure grip, especially during dynamic or high-rep movements. Slick handles, on the other hand, can become slippery as your hands sweat—raising the risk of losing your grip, Pack adds. If you’re training with kettlebell that has a slick grip, consider using workout chalk or liquid chalk during moves like swings.

To choose the best kettlebells, I consulted three personal trainers who regularly work with kettlebells: Taylor Beebe, CPT, Tyneka Pack, CPT, and Almoni Ellis, CSCS. I also got feedback from Women’s Health fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT, who is a certified trainer.

Based on their feedback, I focused on crucial features to look for in these super versatile strength-training tools. I then tested some of the most popular kettlebells out there. Each was put through a slew of workouts to test its efficiency, durability, weight, material, and grip. Because every person’s budget is different, I made sure to include kettlebells with a range of price points.

She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

It has been revealed that taylor Beebe, CPT, is a personal trainer and kettlebell expert in California. She’s also a national qualifier for USA Powerlifting.

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

#98392. Women Aging Well: Lessons From Memories and Reflections

Women Aging Well: Lessons From Memories and Reflections

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • According to recent reports, in Tennessee, I walked a magnificent labyrinth inspired by a clock, formed with 1,000 feet of stone, designed as a space of reflection and connection.
  • As I get older, I am more aware that the path in is never the same as the path out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

According to recent reports, in Tennessee, I walked a magnificent labyrinth inspired by a clock, formed with 1,000 feet of stone, designed as a space of reflection and connection. The artist, Thea Alvin, titled her installation "Time for Love." Since I’ve been thinking about the importance of time as we age, I wandered slowly and quietly on the spiral path toward its center, open to whatever thoughts and feelings emerged. Immediately I relaxed, knowing I would arrive at the center, stay a while, and return along the same path.

As I get older, I am more aware that the path in is never the same as the path out. No path is ever the same because of changes in weather, light, time of day, and the path itself. I am not the same. Just as we can never step in the same river twice, we can never walk along the same path because neither we nor the path remain the same. We evolve over time; as we age, we are continuously unfolding and hopefully, moving toward self-discovery and a center of calm.

I experienced entering the labyrinth as an opportunity to be open and curious about my life at this moment. I have always been drawn to spiral shapes as they are often associated with evolution and transformation. As a nature lover, I notice spiral shapes of pinecones, sunflowers, and other life forms. As I walked the spiral path, I heard the wind, the birdsongs, and the crunching gravel underneath my feet. I listened deeply to myself, without judgment or criticism. When a thought or feeling surfaced, I attempted to observe it and see what it meant. I stayed with that thought and waited to see what else emerged. These were my mind’s musings as I walked to the center. Cultivating curiosity and willingness to stay with a thought or feeling as we age can help us deepen awareness about ourselves, our relationships, and hopefully, encourage us to examine the choices we make in our daily lives.

In a recent development, at the center, I sat on a boulder under a Beech tree, contemplating "Time For Love." The structure was commissioned as a space for family members to come, sit, and remember their loved one who died. The place feels sacred. In my reflection, I recalled people and pets I’ve loved over the course of my life. I felt the warmth of those memories. I realized how much I enjoy reminiscing in this way; quietly, in nature, experiencing sadness and joy. As Thea Alvin intended, I was allocating "Time for Love." Noticing an internal shift, I recognized the necessity of giving myself this time for reflection on love. I needed to do this, and asked myself: How do I use my time compared to how I want to spend it?

Recent findings suggest that those questions stayed with me as I walked out of the labyrinth. I realized that this thought was not just inspired by the labyrinth but also by Varun Soni, Dean of Religious Life at USC, who spoke at a conference I attended about children and spirituality. He asked: “What deserves more of our attention?” “What would we like to make room for?” “What small change regarding our time could we make today?”.

These are notable questions to consider at any age; particularly when we are in our older years, when we are more aware of the time that has passed in relation to the time we may have ahead. The final question Dean Soni asked was “What can we do to change what we discover?” Sitting on a rock, under a tree, in the center of "Time for Love," I realized that I can dedicate time to feel the love that I had in my life, and to actively cultivate the love that I feel now. How will I make more time for love? I will remember those I loved; engage in activities I love, be with people I love, share love in ways that make others feel loved, and engage in acts of loving kindness.

Industry observers note that as I returned along the spiral path, I felt different. I was different. I discovered that actively engaging with love deserves more of my time and attention. And in making this change, I will feel this connection to love as a vital, positive force in my own aging.

Industry observers note that teichman, S., Pearson, R., Cook, W. A., & Banerjee, A. (2026). Contemplative Training for Mindful Aging: Insights from a Study of Participants' Experiences in a Mind-Body Training Course. Canadian Journal on Aging, 45(2), 263–272.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Recent findings suggest that someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so anyone can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, helping the home cook elevate their kitchen experience.

In a recent development, there are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, plus sauces and cookbooks.

It has been revealed that seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

In a recent development, A substantial mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display shows how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

In a recent development, sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker reveals time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

In a recent development, thermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

The Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

According to recent reports, freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The tech giant claims the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

Industry observers note that A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT claims it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

Softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the company will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

Someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Sources indicate that tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Industry observers note that learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Industry observers note that carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and says it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

In a recent development, smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

Old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the company’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

In a recent development, cooking pancakes in a skillet is a solitary affair. If you’re the cook and don’t want to force cold coasters on everyone, you’re standing alone and eating last. Unless you have this new griddle, that is. This 12-pound rectangle spans two burners and stays put, providing an 18.5-by-9.8-inch cooking surface and two heat zones, so you can cook a bunch of pancakes, or eggs and bacon, simultaneously, which means everyone eats together. The carbon steel is nitrided, which means it resists rust and scratches without the need for questionable coatings. Plus, it arrives pre-seasoned with a surface that will only become more non-stick with proper use and care. Plus, a raised lip and rounded corners keep grease in while making it easy to pour off. It’s a great choice whether you’re cooking at the stovetop, in an oven, on a grill, or over a campfire.

According to recent reports, A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

Microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday says the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow says the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

According to recent reports, uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the significant chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

According to recent reports, A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water swiftly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

Industry observers note that most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

According to recent reports, so you know someone with a grinder, a pour-over cone, a French press, a cold brew pitcher, and a milk frother. But sometimes they need a coffee before they can face making coffee. And that’s where this indulgently overengineered Swiss superautomatic espresso maker comes in. The second-generation Z10 has a menu of 51 drinks you can choose and customize through the 4.3-inch touchscreen. Just pour beans into the hopper and fill the water tank. Drinks include classic hot options, as well as “cold brew,” which, while not true long-immersion, is still nice for ice thanks to unheated water pulsing through a coarser grind. With milk or without. But now there are also light selections, plus caffeine regulation levels, as well as sweet foam picks (with a $35 chocolate attachment sold separately). And the upgraded P.R.G.2+ grinder resets itself for each offering, dialing in optimized granule consistency so you never have to worry you’ll have bad luck with a puck. Sure, it’s a splurge, but think of all the time and space someone will save replacing all those other coffee contraptions.

Most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the company calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Industry observers note that matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

Recent findings suggest that pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one manufacturer’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so proposal on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

It has been revealed that nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

It has been revealed that centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the tech giant says fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Recent findings suggest that boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

In a recent development, fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum claims it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Industry observers note that bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

Sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

HexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad states the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

Detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

Stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney states works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

Neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

Sources indicate that chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide says it can go in the dishwasher, though the tech giant’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

Industry observers note that most microwaves cook by guesswork, and the most interaction you have is five beeps and the sighs/screams when things are too cold in the middle and hot at the edges. This sleek Japanese Microwave from Panasonic, however, uses its latest Genius Sensor 2.0 to constantly measure 64 points on your food’s surface every 0.1 seconds, so one button push can achieve even temperature throughout a plate of mixed leftovers. And steady inverter power ensures the center heats, too. The drop-down door, like a wall oven, suits even a narrow galley kitchen (aka many Asian apartments), while the flat, turntable-free interior can fit up to a 9-by-13 dish. This recent import is a 2026 Red Dot Design winner for a reason: it’s got a look as tasty as your bowl of steamy soup.

Want that perfectly fluffy restaurant rice at home, but without under- or over-cooking anxiety and hot-spot drama? Get a Zojirushi rice cooker. I’ve given the NS-ZCC10 Neuro Fuzzy Logic model as a graduation/housewarming gift multiple times because I knew from personal experience it delivers year after year. Then I got this pressure + induction cooker in 2025 and daaaaaaamn … somehow the best got better. Sticky-plump sushi or stir-fry grains, pleasingly textured oatmeal, brown rice that doesn’t take all of eternity. No sad, beige cement. This tiny, calm chef quietly adjusts the heat to deliver evenly cooked everything. It’s not as fast as some cookers, but it beats them in consistency. Fill to the line, press a button, go live life, come back to perfection. This is an upgrade that quietly, magically improves your entire kitchen rhythm.

We’ve wasted so many herbs. You buy basil with such good intentions, but two recipes and three days later, there’s still so much that’s wilted and wasted. Same can be remarked for other greens. And maybe you know someone in the same situation. One “simple” solution is for them to grow their own greens, but not everyone has room for a garden. And what about winter … Well, that’s where this egg-shaped enclosure comes in. Using NASA-inspired nutrient-infused fogponics (way more exciting to watch than standard hydroponics), anyone can grow lettuce or kale or cherry tomatoes, etc., from pre-seeded pods/reusable germination domes, and do it year-round. Just put the indoor garden in a side room, garage, basement, etc., (grow lights can get pretty bright), connect it to Wi-Fi with the Plantaform app, and give it water when an alert tells you. Then, in a few weeks, harvest time! Seasonings season! Garnishes galore! Just clean it well, and you’ll be able to keep good produce on the cutting board, not in the compost. Literally rinse and repeat.

Industry observers note that coffee nerds have so much in common with audiophiles. Both are obsessed with micro-calibrated gear and swapping components in and out in the pursuit of clarity. So if you know someone as obsessed with puck preparation as they are running a carbon-fiber anti-static brush over every album, you know someone who needs the Mazzer Philos premium light commercial single-dose grinder. Like a summit-fi digital audio converter, this $1,495 hand-assembled, heirloom-quality Italian appliance (available in black and silver) takes whatever beans it’s fed and extracts previously masked tasting notes with minimal morning commotion. A wide dial covers espresso to pour-over to batch brew coarseness, and the near-zero-retention vertical burr + chute knocker + Dose Finisher system lets you move between origins and brewing methods without yesterday’s beans staging a comeback. Swappable 64mm flat burrs give someone a chance to tune for vibrant light and full-bodied dark roasts, and the option to switch from stepped to stepless mode gives grind settings the same obsessive precision as establishing the perfect listening position.

South Korea isn’t a casual getaway. But you can still get some Seoul in your soul (food) at home with this set of sauces from three-Michelin-star chef Mingoo Kang of Mingles restaurant and James Beard Award winner Nadia Cho. Fermented slowly in onggi (traditional Korean clay jars that are buried in the hills), and branded with the Korean word for artisan, these sauces are so much better than the red plastic tub of industrial soybean-chili paste you’d pick up at the store (but I still got love for you, H Mart). Start by stirring the deep heat of cooking sauce into marinades, dressings, and/or broths, then use the finishing sauce to glaze meats, or drizzle some zest onto eggs, rice, or dumplings. Whether a chef you know prefers marinara or bibimbap, give them the gift of earthenware alchemy.

Sources indicate that nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

We all have friends who would rather be outdoors than just about anywhere else—always happiest splitting wood, tackling projects around the property, or heading out for a weekend adventure. This holiday season, why not give them something that matches their passion? With a massive lineup of cold-weather work gear, rugged apparel, and outdoor-recreation essentials, Tractor Supply Co. has gifts for every type of adventurer on your list.

Recent findings suggest that lightweight but durable, compact but substantial enough for toddlers, teens, and adults, the Sun Dolphin saucer is a ticket to hours of winter memories. It’s got a glossy surface for maximum slide-ability, built-in handles for holding on tight, and good resistance to cold-weather impacts. Get the three-pack for a family who loves to spend time in the snow.

Industry observers note that available in solids, heathers, and space dyes, this stretchable, loose-fit sweatshirt provides layering for additional warmth without feeling restrictive. And don’t let the ultra-comfortable soft cotton blend fool you: It’s built with Carhartt’s legendary triple-stitch construction for time-tested toughness.

Cold weather doesn’t keep outdoorsy types inside; it just changes what they wear. This sleek hooded puffer, available in Antique Green and Coral, is an excellent layering piece for winter fun. From impromptu picnics to beach days and outdoor concerts, the Field & Stream Vintage Blanket is an easy grab-and-go essential. Its classic vintage-inspired design makes it a stylish companion for spreading out on the grass, lounging outdoors, or packing along for your next adventure.

It has been revealed that these environmentally safe hand warmers will extend their cold-weather fun, from sledding and skiing to skating and fishing and much more. Just open the wrapper, shake the air-activated pouch briefly, and slip it inside gloves, mittens, or pockets.

Whether you’re camping, fishing, hiking, or spending a weekend at the campsite, a reliable multi-tool is an outdoor essential worth keeping close. The Gerber Suspension-NXT packs multiple handy tools into one compact design, making it easy to bring along for everything from campsite setups to unexpected fixes on the trail.

Chances are the nature lover on your list picks up their share of nicks and cuts on their adventures. Great for kids and parents alike, these playful adhesive bandages are latex-free and gentle on sensitive skin, taking some of the sting out of the scrapes they get along the way.

According to recent reports, treat bites and stings without creams or chemicals with this lightweight, easy-to-use, highly portable device. It applies instant heat to help reduce swelling and itching, and comes with a handy carabiner for clipping to backpacks, camping gear, or travel bags.

Inside Sam Bankman-Fried’s $35 Million Bahamas Crypto HQ

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four years after the fall of cryptocurrency partners-in-crime Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, their Icarian story is coming to the small screen twice over.
  • No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.
  • Industry observers note that bankman-Fried and Ellison met while working at trading firm Jane Street in Manhattan in 2016, and began an on-again, off-again romantic relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four years after the fall of cryptocurrency partners-in-crime Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, their Icarian story is coming to the small screen twice over. A docuseries about the scandal, The Boy Who Stole Millions?, debuts on Prime Video November 30, and Netflix’s drama series The Altruists premiered November 19.

No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.

The Orchid building at Albany, The Bahamas.

Industry observers note that bankman-Fried and Ellison met while working at trading firm Jane Street in Manhattan in 2016, and began an on-again, off-again romantic relationship. Bankman-Fried’s first crypto business was the quantitative trading firm he cofounded in 2017, Alameda Research. He went on to found crypto exchange FTX. Ellison, who first began working at Alameda in 2018, became its co-CEO and ran the firm as FTX’s hedge fund.

Bankman-Fried and Ellison moved to The Bahamas in 2021, reportedly motivated by looser COVID-19 pandemic protocols, and “a proactive stance taken by The Bahamas and its regulatory bodies on cryptocurrencies,” Bankman-Fried told Blockworks.

The FTX and Alameda crews encamped at a luxury resort community called Albany. (Tiger Woods and Justin Timberlake are both investors.) Through his companies, Bankman-Fried purchased a penthouse in the sleek Orchid building there, named for its custom cutout façade. Designed by Morris Adjmi Architects, the Orchid’s blue latticework (inspired by New Orleans ironwork), is unmissable, offering an open-air feel to residents while signaling a layer of privacy to outsiders.

A reception area in the Orchid building.

According to recent reports, bankman-Fried shared his 11,500-square-foot unit with Ellison and eight other FTX and Alameda employees. The apartment has a circular living room, a light-up bar, Italian marble floors, cove lighting, and custom closets. Per a real estate listing obtained by Semafor, Bankman-Fried’s unit had German-engineered windows and doors. Outdoor amenities included a firepit, spa, grill and cooking area, and pool.

The couple attempted to evade culpability for misappropriating $8 billion of FTX customer money, a crime uncovered after Bankman-Fried bought his Bahamas property. Both were convicted of wire fraud and several conspiracy charges. Ellison served 14 months of a 24-month sentence. Bankman-Fried is presently serving a 25-year prison sentence and maintains that he is innocent.

Recent findings suggest that to bring this story to life for The Altruists, production designer Todd Fjelsted re-created the infamous penthouse. Several interiors were shot in Vancouver, but scenes requiring a beach or docks were shot in the Dominican Republic.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in a scene from The Altruists filmed in the Orchid set.

Fjelsted and his crew also built miniature replicas of real Albany buildings and a marina complete with a 10-foot remote-control yacht, using forced perspective to shoot them as backdrops. He calls this “the anti-AI set.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the dramatization, coworkers trade crypto in a communal office and party on a balcony overlooking the water. An employee in a hot tub bangs a gong for rounds of speed chess played on fancy sets. Inside, gaming is a major pastime, and there’s a baby grand piano on hand, though no one plays it. In real life, it was reported that Bankman-Fried kept a bean bag under the piano for napping.

Alex Lawther as Sam Trabucco and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

In a recent development, looking to humanize the leads, Fjelsted observed how “insecurities [and] their feelings of a little bit of an imposter syndrome” informed Sam and Caroline’s design choices or lack thereof. Neutrals, sea colors, and palm tree prints made for a better on-camera look, but in real FBI interior photos, Fjelsted saw bedroom walls with powder blue sponge-painted over navy.

Garner and Boyle as Ellison and Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

Throughout the show’s eight episodes, the penthouse goes from bustling with the excitement of trading to vibrating with panic as the scandal comes crashing down. Eventually, the space is left nearly empty, with just Bankman-Fried and his parents remaining. In 2024, it was reported that Bankman-Fried’s real estate holdings would be sold off in order to pay back his debts, and today, the unit is indeed up for sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a new Taycan or Macan EV. In fact, it’s not even a full-sized car. Instead, the German automaker has teamed up with British luxury miniature car builder Hedley Studios to create an 80%-scale electric replica of one of Porsche’s most iconic racing cars, the legendary 550 Spyder.

Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.

Sources indicate that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the company before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company. Among its more entertaining projects was a life-sized recreation of the famous Japanese Tamiya Wild One RC dune buggy, turning a childhood remote-controlled favorite into an actual drivable electric vehicle. We’ve also covered the company’s ultra-luxurious miniature electric cars, including its stunning Bentley Blower recreation.

Now the manufacturer has turned its attention to Porsche, and the result is perhaps its most impressive miniature EV yet.

There’s something I love about miniature electric cars, combining the fun of four-wheels with the right-sized (or pint-sized) magic of mini-mobility.

The Porsche 550 J is based on the original 550 Spyder, Porsche’s first purpose-built racing sports car, which debuted in 1953 and went on to become a motorsport legend.

Despite being scaled down to 80% of the original’s dimensions, the upcoming electric version still seats two adults. It weighs just 350 kg (772 lb), thanks partly to its lightweight tubular steel spaceframe and hand-formed carbon fiber bodywork.

The standard version features an 8 kW (11 hp) electric motor operating on a 48V system, providing a top speed of 40 mph (65 km/h) and a range of up to 30 miles (50 km).

In a recent development, for those who want a bit more performance from their miniature Porsche, an optional RS Pack doubles the power to 16 kW (21 hp), increases the top speed to 50 mph (80 km/h), and extends the range to 50 miles (80 km) thanks to additional batteries. The upgrade also includes drilled disc brakes and adjustable suspension.

The attention to detail goes well beyond the exterior. The car features Brembo brakes, Bilstein suspension, Continental tires, and even a wood-rimmed Nardi steering wheel, just like the original. The classic dashboard retains its three-dial layout, though the fuel gauge has been replaced with a battery meter and the original choke lever now serves as a drive mode selector.

Even the charging port is cleverly hidden beneath the chrome fuel filler cap.

The project was developed in close collaboration with Porsche over six years, with Hedley Studios gaining access to original engineering drawings, archival materials, and historic vehicles in Porsche’s museum.

Only 250 examples will be produced, with buyers able to choose historic racing liveries or custom paint finishes, including colors matching their full-sized Porsches.

Of course, this level of craftsmanship doesn’t come cheap. Prices start at £69,500 (approximately US $91,000), before taxes and options. Orders are already open through Porsche dealers and Hedley Studios, with deliveries expected to begin in spring 2027.

That’s a lot of money for a car that’s only 80% there, but then again, this isn’t really meant to be practical transportation. It’s a collector’s piece that just happens to be electric, drivable, and capable of hitting 50 mph. When there are only 250 of these being built, the £70k price is really just the entry ticket to a special, ultra-luxury club of electric mini-Porsches.

Recent findings suggest that and if you ask me, that sounds like a pretty fun combination. I don’t think I’ll ever be in the market for one of these personally, but I’d sure love to be friends with someone who is!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, an isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home.
  • New research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons.
  • In a recent development, our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, major cats, and even eagles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

New research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

In a recent development, our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, major cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

Recent findings suggest that in this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

Recent findings suggest that “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, mentioned in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

Recent findings suggest that with these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

According to recent reports, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

To defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what upcoming ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.
