💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • Officials proposal to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • Industry observers note that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials proposal to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

Industry observers note that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

In a recent development, korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with fresh tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

According to recent reports, the sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han claims he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

It has been revealed that “I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place new anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never remarked he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be newly introduced concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Recent findings suggest that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV — for its top crowdfunder

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022.
  • Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it indicates it needs to start series production.

Aptera announced today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.

According to recent reports, accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.

Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.

In the release, Hartono said Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the organization is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.

No number was given for how many more.

Sources indicate that the timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million, down from $40 to $45 million, and said the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”.

Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing says substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”.

In a recent development, on November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.

In a recent development, the solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.

The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.

Sources indicate that credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this company since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.

A positive achievement, but the question remains: Is this essentially a hand-built prototype and a token delivery to one very rich customer, or is it the first of many more vehicles that will roll off an assembly line for regular people over the next couple months?

But I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it indicates it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.

The real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera says it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.

Recent findings suggest that we want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

It has been revealed that if you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, even if your car doesn’t have panels built into the body like the Aptera. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. Industry News: 5 Ways To Prioritize Your Brain Health

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the body’s most vital organs—the brain—can be overlooked, even though it guides nearly everything we do.
  • In a recent development, at its core, brain health is about how well your body’s command center functions—processing emotions, coordinating movement, and interpreting what you see, hear, taste, touch, and smell.
  • Because the brain plays such a central role in everyday life, you don’t have to wait until something feels off to start taking care of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sponsored by Eli Lilly and Tech giant.

One of the body’s most vital organs—the brain—can be overlooked, even though it guides nearly everything we do.

In a recent development, at its core, brain health is about how well your body’s command center functions—processing emotions, coordinating movement, and interpreting what you see, hear, taste, touch, and smell. It also includes cognitive health—your ability to think, learn, and remember.

Because the brain plays such a central role in everyday life, you don’t have to wait until something feels off to start taking care of it. Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease can begin about 20 years before symptoms appear, making a proactive approach to brain health an notable part of caring for your overall health.

This messaging inspired actress, author, and advocate Julianne Moore to partner with Eli Lilly and Manufacturer on their Brain Health Matters campaign to encourage people to prioritize their brain health. “From my conversations with people living with Alzheimer’s disease, I’ve seen how much proactive care matters,” Moore indicates. “That’s why I’m helping to encourage everyone to prioritize their brain health through regular conversations with their doctors.”.

Sources indicate that not sure where to begin? Here are five ways to make brain health a priority part in your overall health.

You might not have any concerns about cognitive decline, much less dementia. But taking a proactive approach to cognitive health doesn’t have to wait until later in life—or until something feels off. One brain change associated with Alzheimer’s disease involves amyloid, a protein the body produces naturally. Talking to your doctor can help you understand your personal risk factors and discuss whether steps such as establishing a cognitive baseline and adopting brain-healthy habits may be appropriate for you.

Add brain health to your “must-ask” list for medical appointments and come prepared with specific questions to guide the conversation. Ask your doctor whether a cognitive assessment is appropriate for you. This spoken, written, or digital evaluation can provide a starting point for monitoring your memory and thinking over time.

While a cognitive assessment cannot diagnose a condition on its own, establishing a baseline and completing follow-up assessments as recommended by your doctor may help spot early signs of memory and thinking challenges and monitor changes over time.

Here’s what you may want to ask your doctor:.

Sources indicate that research shows that up to 45 percent of dementia cases, including those caused by Alzheimer’s disease, may be prevented or delayed by managing changeable risk factors. These include blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes; lifestyle habits around diet, exercise, alcohol consumption, and smoking; and even hearing loss, depression, traumatic brain injury (TBI), and sleep.

Recent findings suggest that you can’t change everything that affects your risk—such as age, family history, or certain genetic markers. But your doctor can help you understand the risk factors that may apply to you and build a strategy to manage those that can be changed. The following brain-healthy habits can be a good place to start:.

Once you understand your risk factors, establish a cognitive baseline, and identify brain-healthy habits that could work for you, the next step is bringing those pieces together. Work with your doctor to create a plan based on your individual health needs.

Your blueprint might include ways to manage changeable risk factors, behaviors that support your brain health, and a schedule for revisiting your cognitive health with your doctor. Regular conversations with your doctor about these topics can help you take action early and help support your brain health for the future.

Honest discussions around brain health can help go a long way toward reducing stigma and helping others feel more comfortable seeking information, support, and care. Opening up—even in small ways—can make a difference, whether you’re checking in with loved ones, sharing your own concerns, or simply normalizing the topic in everyday life.

“Brain health is something we don’t talk about often enough,” Moore says. “There’s so much fear around cognitive health and even talking to a doctor about getting an assessment. I think it needs to be normalized.”.

To learn more about how you can be proactive for your brain health, visit BrainHealthMatters.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

In a recent development, fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

According to recent reports, “Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo remarked in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”.

According to recent reports, the zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

It has been revealed that even though your holiday tree (probably) only comes out once a year, choosing the right artificial Christmas tree for your home is important to set a truly festive vibe. If you’re already committed to the faux lifestyle or are just dipping your toes in, the perfect tree is out there for you and your priorities. Maybe you want something bold and full of personality like the iconic Rockefeller tree in Fresh York City. Perhaps you’re looking to go classic with a full lighting system included or something to match your favorite wreaths. No matter your preference, there’s a good chance that once you go faux, you’re never going back to the real deal. After all, there’s no watering involved, cleanup is a breeze, and easy storage is usually part of the design.

Our list below includes pre-lit trees that take the guesswork out of nostalgic spruces and even an enticing winter white design. And to really achieve a professional-looking holiday home, we’ve tapped experts like Kendall Jenner’s holiday floral designer Jeff Leatham and AD-darling designer Shea McGee for exclusive tips on how to level up any faux tree.

Reviewer: Divya Viswanathan, VP, commerce portfolio lead.

This significant, beautiful tree is inspired by the Fraser Fir. Known for its rich, dark green coloring and full silhouette, this tree is native to the Appalachian Mountains and has the distinction of being the type of tree most often used as the official White House Christmas tree.

Sources indicate that to be honest, we can’t tell the difference between Balsam Hill’s faux version and the real thing. BH's impressive “true needle” foliage features 40 variations of branch types throughout and the effect is incredibly realistic.

The tree is available just about any height and light variation you could want, all of which feature an easy plug system. Easy plug trees have all the light strands plugged into the center pole, so all you have to do is place the three sections together and plug the tree into an outlet. There’s no need to ever unplug or take off any light strands.

In a recent development, the style pictured above is “color + clear,” which allows you to switch between multicolored lights and white lights via remote. For pre-lit trees with a single lighting style, there is an attached foot pedal to turn the lights on and off. The Twinkly light style features built-in app-controlled smart lights from Twinkly.

The tree features hinged branches, making setup and teardown straightforward (just push each hinge down and pop into a storage bag). If you’re looking for a large tree, and a full tree but don’t want to spend a fortune, this is a good, solid pick from The National Tree Tech giant. The National Tree Company has been making holiday trees and decorations for more than 60 years, and they have plenty more styles to choose from on Amazon and Wayfair.

Personally, I think the color of the tree should be a bit darker with a somewhat brown undertone to make it look more natural than a solid evergreen.

Industry observers note that shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher’s Treetopia prelit faux balsam was a big upgrade from her under-$100 Best Choice pick that’s also named on this list. While Arzbaecher noted in her review that the Best Choice option is “nice enough if you’re looking to get a larger tree on a budget,” it didn’t really achieve a realistic appearance: “Up close, the look of the branches on this tree read less like needles and more like green fringe,” she told us. At $200, Treetopia’s artificial tree is still considered one of the “budget options” on our list, but Arzbaecher noticed quite a difference. “My old tree was incredibly sparse (we’re talking putting Charlie Brown to shame) so this is definitely an upgrade,” she indicates. “The branch tips go about ¾ of the way in towards the center of each section, which makes it appear fuller. It may have even converted me to a pre-lit devotee.”.

Reviewer: Emma Tubbs, audience development manager.

According to recent reports, how easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? 6.

According to recent reports, how long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? The most time-consuming part of the assembly process was unfurling and fluffing the tree, but there was very minimal needle loss. I spent about 40 minutes setting it up but roughly 35 minutes of that was fluffing the many sections. The lights that came already incorporated into the tree were twisted around each section very tightly, so I had to spend a good amount of time untangling the lights so that I could fully fluff it up.

Sources indicate that did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? The tree came pre-lit, which is nice, but as I remarked, the lights were wrapped so tightly that it took a bit to loosen them so I could fluff the tree. I’m giving it an 8 since it did save some time that it came pre-lit, but it wasn’t totally seamless.

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? Yes, it definitely lived up to my expectations! I specifically wanted a slimmer tree so I wouldn’t have to rearrange my living room too much, and this was the perfect width. The 7.5-foot height is perfect for my tall ceiling, and the tree is slim but still full and realistic-looking so it doesn’t look gangly.

How full is the tree (scale of 1-10, with 10 being the fullest)? 6—since the tree is intentionally more slim and compact, it’s not luxuriously full, but once fluffed up, you can’t see any of the inner metal parts that might make it look artificial otherwise.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? 6—up close, you can see that the needles are plastic, but the overall fullness and structure of the tree make it look authentic otherwise. The metal components that make up the frame are hidden in the interior column, which definitely helps. The base is metal and clearly artificial, but I always put a skirt around my tree (even when I’ve had a real one) so that aspect is also naturally concealed.

Puleo International is another well-known name in the artificial tree game, selling at outlets like Amazon, Wayfair, Home Depot, and Lowe's. The brand’s slim Fraser fir was exactly what tester Emma Tubbs was after: “I wanted a slimmer tree so I wouldn’t have to rearrange my living room too much, and this was the perfect width,” she states. The tree’s versatile look and approachable price point also helped it overtake the Best Choice Products Pencil Christmas Tree for our ‘Best Slim Tree’ pick. “The 7.5-foot height is perfect for my tall ceiling, and the tree is slim but still full and realistic-looking so it doesn’t look gangly,” says Tubbs.

Industry observers note that we always research products thoroughly before including them, and test every single one. Our reviews are thorough, in-depth, and honest. We put ourselves in the shoes of the shopper (because most of the time, we are the ones shopping!), and make sure that we’re answering the questions that we would want answered in the buying process.

Industry observers note that we favored natural-looking trees that are easy to set up. We also took shipping into account and tested trees that arrive not only in style, but with speed.

Industry observers note that all trees that were reviewed were unboxed, set up (and lit up) by our contributors. They lived with trees and experienced all they had to offer firsthand, so that they could share the real deal with our readers.

What Size Christmas Tree Is Right for Me?

First and foremost, the height of your fake Christmas tree should depend on the height of your ceiling. A good rule of thumb is to keep your tree at least one-and-a-half feet lower than your ceiling, otherwise, it will look crowded. “I like to leave about six to12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in,” states Shea McGee (more on the designer’s holiday advice below). Both McGee and Jeff Leatham, the floral designer who helped mastermind Kendall Jenner’s festive holiday house, agree that seven to eight feet hits a sweet spot in most homes. “The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe,” says McGee.

Who Should Buy Fake Christmas Trees?

According to recent reports, some people want to avoid the hassle (and extra cost) of buying a fresh tree each year, while others are allergic to real trees or are concerned about the fire safety hazard that comes along with real trees (they can become highly flammable as they dry out). Others (including people with pets) know that a real Christmas tree can be bait for disaster. Fresh or faux is really a matter of personal preference, and anyone who wants a fake Christmas tree should go for it. Leatham points out that in faux trees, the branches don’t drop, the coloring stays vibrant, and there’s often more structure to add extra ornaments.

Is It Better to Get a Pre-Lit Tree Or to Do It Yourself?

Choosing if you want your tree pre-lit is one of the first decisions you’ll make when navigating the vast artificial tree world. Pre-lit options are the preference of holiday decor gurus like Leatham. “Always, always, always go for prelit—it makes the tree look more full and realistic,” he tells us. Our editors like that pre-lit Christmas trees are convenient to set up (opposed to blindly garlanding string lights) and how they help guarantee your lighting scheme will look uniform. That said, drawbacks include potentially difficult repairs. While you can easily unstring removable lights to troubleshoot, built-in LEDs might pose bigger technical challenges. On the other hand, stringing your own lights may be a more complex, time-consuming process, but you’ll ultimately have more control over which areas of your tree are spotlighted.

How Should You Decorate Your Christmas Tree?

You’ve gotten your tree up, fluffed the branches, and poured yourself a nice cup of hot cocoa or eggnog to celebrate—now comes the fun part: decorating. While there’s no right way to decorate your Christmas tree, we looked through our archives for some tips and tricks to give your setup some extra sparkle.

Industry observers note that if your mentality is “more is more,” your holiday hero will be Kathy Hilton, who greeted AD back in 2021 with four artificial Christmas trees decked out with all the bells and whistles (emphasis on the bells). One tip we’d steal from Hilton is the idea that the decorations don’t have to go up all at once. “I normally start decorating in October, then keep adding until December,” claims Hilton.

Kendall Jenner, on the other hand, favors a more traditional tree, dipped in nostalgic classics like tinsel, twinkle lights, and vintage Christopher Radko ornaments that were passed down by her mother, Kris. Her designer reveals that she even loves stringing popcorn for the tree and dried orange slices on garlands. “Every year, more and more of my clients want more traditional holiday decorations that they can invest in, collect, and pass on to other generations,” indicates Leatham. “I love that idea of seeing the same ornaments every year and having them bring back wonderful memories.” Since we have a feeling you have your own collection of heirloom Christmas decorations that have been collecting dust, we’d look to the supermodel for inspiration.

Recent findings suggest that color scheming your ornament display is one way to set yourself apart from the pack. “Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” claims Annie Sloan, color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. Stylist Dorcia Kelley of Kelle Miles Studio also suggests using a planter instead of a traditional tree stand or skirt for a modern look. “When hanging ornaments, you want to make sure you’re hanging it towards the end of the branch instead of right at the tip. This way, they’ll be more stable,” she says.

We also recommend playing with shapes, textures, and finishes to create as much interest as possible. AD’s perfect Christmas tree (pictured at the top of this article) features lots of vintage-inspired John Derian ornaments that bring on the kitsch, accented with classic ball ornaments in a range of sizes to create depth and dimension. A color palette of muted blue and bold metallic hues complement the deep green branches while slivers of silver tinsel add holiday pizzazz.

Fluffing your artificial Christmas tree is the key to convincingly faking the real thing. Most of the time, your tree will arrive with all the branches up-turned straight out of the box, and you’ll first want to mount the tree in its stand or collar. Next comes the actual fluffing—as reviewer Pujah Shah mentioned, it’s a smart idea to wear some work gloves to avoid any pricking that might occur while you’re working through the branches. Starting at the bottom, you’ll fan the largest branches down, layer by layer, until you reach the very top (where the branches become much shorter). If your branches have smaller tips built in, we like the center-right-left method of starting toward the base of the tree and positioning the smaller tips first center, next towards the right, and lastly towards the left, until you’ve reached the end. After that, you’ll go branch by branch, noticing that your tree looks full and much more lush with each adjustment. Afterwards, all that’s left to do is make any minor fixes to eliminate bald spots and voila!

What’s the Best Real Christmas Tree to Buy?

According to recent reports, again, that’s completely a matter of personal preference. Trees come in a variety of hues, some with a dark green, some with a blue tint, and others with a bright shade. Some have spiky needles while others are soft to the touch. Trees vary by geographical region and what's native to your area, but some of the most popular options used as Christmas trees across the U.S. include the Fraser Fir, Balsam Fir, Douglas Fir, and Blue Spruce (all of which are available in faux varieties, as well!).

How Does the Lifetime Cost of a Faux Tree Compare to Annually Buying a Real Tree?

In a recent development, while how much your real Christmas tree costs will vary depending on its size as well as where you live in the United States, expect to spend anywhere from $40 to well over $100. In a few years, that running total will start to cost you, but with an artificial tree, you’ll pay the total cost up front. High-quality trees can also last you up to 15 years, making the sometimes extravagant price tags more digestible, especially in the later years when you’re no longer burdened with figuring out the logistics of strapping that netted Douglas Fir onto the car roof.

What Is Flocking and How Do You Do It?

Sources indicate that flocking refers to the process of dusting your artificial Christmas tree with a powdery white overcoat to mimic the appearance of fresh snowfall. Some trees—like the Yaheetech tree Brie Schwartz tested—come pre-flocked, but if you prefer a DIY moment, ready-to-flock sprays are also available at most substantial box retailers. We like Balsam Hill’s guide to flocking your tree, which details a recipe for homemade flocking, as well as all the safety precautions you’ll want to take: Like wearing protective gear, flocking in a well-ventilated environment, and ensuring you’re using non-hazardous materials. (Though if your budget allows, we think it might be best to invest in one of the brand’s ready-flocked trees.).

King of Christmas vs. Balsam Hill.

In a recent development, in the grand scheme of artificial Christmas trees, King of Christmas and Balsam Hill are widely known as the crème de la crème, thanks to their realistic appearance, convenient setup, and thoughtful extras like complimentary storage bags for the off-season. While both fall into the category of more luxuriously-priced holiday decor, Balsam Hill’s price points are slightly higher ($349 to $4,000+ while King of Christmas ranges from $229 to $3,000+).

Recent findings suggest that in our own quests for the most elite faux trees, we’ve also tried both brands. Commerce vice president Divya Viswanathan called Balsam Hill’s Fraser Fir “the Christmas tree of my dreams,” while contributor Andrea Lewis previously called her Blue Spruce from the brand “a lovely addition to our holiday traditions—elegant, easy to manage, and captures that cozy, Christmas air perfectly.” AD’s global director of audience development Pujah Shah became a King of Christmas convert last holiday after testing the brand’s Alpine Fir tree. “I wanted something tall, sleek, and a little bit dramatic that felt intentional in a modern space but still cozy enough for family chaos—it nails both,” states Shah. We think that both brands are great options—it’s hard to beat how realistic Balsam Hills designs are, and holiday floral designer and one of our experts, Jeff Leatham even named King of Christmas as his favorite brand. To choose the right brand for you, we recommend figuring out what will suit your space and your decorations, as well as establishing a price point you’re comfortable with.

According to recent reports, we tapped the designer and creative force behind one of our favorite interior brands, McGee & Co., on the best ways to make your artificial Christmas tree really pop this season. Read on for her advice on how to make merry with a beautiful, yet intentional holiday set up.

Is There Such a Thing as an Ideal Sized Christmas Tree?

“When you’re choosing a tree, the ideal size really depends on your space. I like to leave about 6–12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in. For most standard spaces, a 7-7.5-foot tree hits the sweet spot. If you have tall ceilings, you can absolutely go bigger—9-12 feet fills the volume beautifully. And in smaller rooms, a slimmer silhouette keeps things festive without overwhelming the layout. The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe.”.

What are Some of the Design Benefits of Choosing an Artificial Christmas Tree Versus a Real One?

Sources indicate that “I love the flexibility an artificial tree gives you. You know exactly what shape and fullness you’re getting, and the branches stay right where you want them—which makes decorating so much easier and more polished. They also hold up all season long, which is great if you like to decorate early. And of course, you can reuse them year after year, which means you can invest in the style you love and bring it back every holiday.”.

How Do You Make an Artificial Christmas Tree Look More Realistic?

“Start with a tree that already has a natural, realistic base—good branch texture goes a long way. From there, keep your palette cohesive so the whole tree feels curated instead of busy. I love layering garlands because they add that organic movement you see in real trees. Then finish with meaningful ornaments, ribbon, and a few organic touches—like dried citrus or pinecones. Those add warmth and authenticity, making even a faux tree feel beautifully lifelike.”.

“Both options have their place. A pre-lit tree is all about ease—the lights are perfectly placed, and you get that warm glow the minute you plug it in. It’s great if you want a beautiful tree without the extra steps. An unlit tree gives you more creative freedom. You can layer different styles of lights, change the mood from year to year, and really customize the look. It takes a bit more time, but it can feel incredibly intentional. So, if you want quick and polished, go pre-lit. If you love the process of styling every detail, unlit is the way to go.”.

According to recent reports, the easiest way to make your artificial Christmas tree look like a real tree is to, well, cover it up. Go heavier on the decorations this year: Think garland, Christmas lights, pinecones, ornaments, a tree topper, etc. We're talking the works. Check out our go-to holiday decor tips that will make the best Christmas trees look even more magical.

Industry observers note that it’s affordable in bulk, doubles as a garland, and covers quite a bit of real estate from low to high. And who doesn’t love a bow? We pulled an option to satisfy the minimalists as well as some embellished trim that’s got major maximalist appeal.

A dead giveaway—no pun intended—that your tree’s a fake is the base: that plastic, mechanical-esque tree stand. Cover that metal stand up with a festive tree skirt (or basket!) as you would with real Christmas trees.

Industry observers note that if your tree doesn’t have pre-strung lights, head to the holiday aisle for some white or multicolored lights. Some of our favorites include unconventional and more delicate-looking lights that don’t necessarily scream “Christmas.” They’ll draw the eye to the center of the tree and take the attention off of the branches. Besides, you can never have too many lights in your home decor during the holiday season.

Recent findings suggest that when scouting out ornaments for your tree, look for options with serious heirloom potential. Kendall Jenner’s Christopher Radko’s classic ornament collection is a good example—and Etsy sellers have troves of vintage ornaments to start your own traditions or recreate the supermodel’s holiday style. These miniature bulbs we found at Terrain are a fun way to create more depth when paired with larger balls, and we like that the different colors really pop when your tree is lit. We also turned to John Derian for gorgeous, traditional options pictured on our tree.

#98364. "What Does This Mean For Me?" When Life Is All About Ourself

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1150 w)

"What Does This Mean For Me?" When Life Is All About Ourself

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • In a recent development, this is part 2 in a series.
  • Industry observers note that we don't interact with our life directly; we interact with what life means about us.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In a recent development, this is part 2 in a series. You can read part 1 here.

Industry observers note that we don't interact with our life directly; we interact with what life means about us. What if the problem isn't that life isn't meeting our needs? What if the problem is that getting our personal needs met has become the single focus of our life?

Sources indicate that in part 1 of this series, I discussed the many ways we’re conditioned and wired to be self-focused in today’s world, to constantly monitor and manage our own okay-ness and whether our needs are being met. And furthermore, how each moment is experienced as what we've decided it says about us. Does this situation, conversation, decision, opinion make me feel less than or better than? Does it make me feel valued, comfortable, seen? Does it validate my story of “who I am”? I posited the idea that viewing our lives through the lens of “does this serve me?” is, at its root, an attempt to be happy, shore ourselves up, and ultimately, survive. While, in fact, we’ve got it wrong: putting “me” at the center of the universe and the reason everything happens ends up making us suffer.

So what exactly is the suffering that comes with our relentless self-focus—what’s wrong with seeing everything through the lens of how it affects “me”?

According to recent reports, when we experience every situation and everyone else's choices through the lens of “self,” as fundamentally a commentary on how we're doing and a referendum on our worth, then every moment carries the potential to wound, undermine, humiliate, and destroy us. Every interaction can threaten who we think we are. We have to remain hyper-vigilant, therefore, on high alert for whether we’re okay or not okay, and any experience that feels like it doesn’t support our story of ourselves, which can also include a simple difference of opinion.

We live in a constant state of “not-enoughness.” We can never get enough approval, recognition, validation, reassurance, success, or reflection. The self that needs to be continually affirmed is never permanently satisfied; whatever we “get” only lasts as long as this particular experience. We imagine that if we win this argument or get this situation to “go our way,” and be “good for us,” we’ll finally get enough affirmation, enough validation to trust our worth and put down our “me” sword. But it never happens; there is no “enough” point, and so we live in a constant state of lack, always trying to get what we need from the outside so we can be okay on the inside.

Our life becomes an endless project dedicated to self-management.

We feel like we have to be constantly improving the project of "me"—making sure we're doing enough and getting enough. Our life becomes a full-time job of managing the person we're trying to be and be seen as. The result is utter exhaustion and burnout.

Recent findings suggest that because we experience other people as threats to our self-story, and see others through the lens of whether their behavior serves or doesn’t serve us, we can’t meet people for real, as they are. We’ve got too much skin in the game. Who they are becomes about who they make us feel we are. And so, we can’t really relax fully and get to know others and give them the space to be who they are as whole beings, independent from us, with their own motivations, desires, wants, and needs that are not about us. All roads lead back to us in some way, which clouds our view of the other. We can’t really listen because we have to constantly monitor and scan for potential threats to who we are. We can’t allow others to have a different opinion or experience from us because it “means” our opinion is wrong and consequently, there’s something wrong with us. Our “me” agenda requires everyone else’s thoughts, opinions, and truth to confirm and align with our “me” project, which is a lot of work since that’s never the case. That said, only some parts of other people are allowed into our relationships, the parts that work for us and give us what we need. But we’re not available to meet or know the whole of them.

According to recent reports, our relationships are, therefore, built on filling our own holes and reassuring our own insecurities—getting what we need to feel good or at least okay. We end up using other people to satisfy and validate ourselves. We give in order to feel appreciated and be valued as helpful. We listen to others in order to be perceived as a good listener and so that we can be listened to. How we relate is driven by how it relates to and reflects on us. Our relationships, therefore, can’t be truly open, honest, and emotionally intimate; we can’t be vulnerable and undefended, and can’t really know others as people in their own right, who they really are separate from us. We remain disconnected, relating to others as merely supporting characters in our personal movie—the movie playing in our me-focused mind.

Because we’re always telling ourselves a story about our life, what it means for us, whether we’re getting what we need, and whether our life is serving the project of “me,” we’re not available to life as it’s actually happening. We’re not in the present moment; we're trapped inside a story we’ve told ourselves about our life and how our “me” is faring in it. At the same time, we’re not truly connected to other people. Other people are characters in our personal movie, and are experienced through the lens of whether they’re filling our needs and making us feel good about ourselves. Other people are not subjects in their own right, but objects who can help support who we think we are.

Industry observers note that our self-focused approach to life is an attempt to keep us happy and secure, but it ends up backfiring, leaving us feeling disconnected from life and other people, enslaved to how we're being perceived. It leaves us defensive and emotionally fragile, vulnerable to other people’s different opinions and experiences, and having to constantly manage the project of “me” and make sure we’re enough.

In part 3, I’ll dive into the profound benefits of dropping “me” from the center of our universe, and the relief that comes when we learn to show up for life without our “me” in the way, and when we can see life as something happening, but without turning it into something happening to, for, and because of us. What if it’s not about us?

How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that coffee consumption among U.S.
  • adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day.
  • By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:.

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:.

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:.

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she stated.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

It has been revealed that “Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:.

Industry observers note that “These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

It has been revealed that she also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick mentioned.

According to recent reports, she suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an vital factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” remarked Kirkpatrick.

Just within the last week, several innovative newly introduced headphones and earbuds have been declared, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

Sources indicate that first up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the latest Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

Sources indicate that the 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

In a recent development, both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously confirmed $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

It has been revealed that compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

It has been revealed that as for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

Industry observers note that the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the tech giant’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

Concerns arose from a single study involving college rugby players who took high creatine doses. This study reported an increase in a testosterone metabolite linked to hair loss. However, it's vital to note that this study was short-term and on a small sample size, not replicated, and the observed variable in the creatine group remained within normal clinical limits.

Other research on creatine and testosterone levels found no significant changes. While the initial study raised questions, there's no solid proof linking creatine to hair loss. So, rest assured, creatine doesn't seem to be the culprit.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when it comes to body recomposition, showing up and crushing your workouts is only half the equation. You also need to pay attention to your nutrition to build muscle and lose fat.

And that part of the job isn’t always as straightforward as exercise. In the gym, you know you need to regularly lift enough to challenge your muscles and get your cardio in. In the kitchen, body recomposition typically involves two key things: getting enough protein and managing your calorie intake. As simple as that sounds, it isn’t always easy.

In a recent development, there are a few ways to approach these goals, but one key to making them more sustainable and manageable (and therefore easier to stick to!) is to track your macronutrients, or macros. The three macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats, and protein, and each plays a unique role in your body recomposition journey.

According to recent reports, carbs get a lot of unnecessary hate, but they’re your body’s primary energy source, says Dana White, RD. Your body relies on glucose, a sugar that is broken down from carbs. Without enough of it, your energy, concentration, and mood can all be affected.

In a recent development, fats are vital to your body’s overall functioning. They support the health of your cells, help your body absorb vitamins like A, D, E, and K, and play a substantial role in satiety, White indicates. Protein, perhaps the most obvious of the three, plays a major role in muscle repair and development—notable at any time, but especially on a body recomp journey.

Counting your macros can help you stay on track with your body recomposition journey. To find out how much of each macro you need and how to fill your plate, try our Eating for Body Recomp Guide.

Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

According to recent reports, for camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

It has been revealed that the ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

Sources indicate that volkswagen will open orders for the new ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

Nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

Recent findings suggest that what about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a upcoming Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

In a recent development, however, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

According to recent reports, the 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

  • The sex and weight have not been revealed yet, and the calf also does not have a name.
  • In a recent development, at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage demonstrates rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been revealed yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

In a recent development, at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she highlighted signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos noted in an e-mailed statement. “It was a substantial moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

Recent findings suggest that both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

“Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

Industry observers note that while not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species right now lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This new calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

Sources indicate that “Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is vital in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

#98357. The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive

The Boon of Being Highly Sensitive

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Are you more easily overstimulated than others by what’s going on around you?
  • We all navigate the world using our senses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Are you more easily overstimulated than others by what’s going on around you? Maybe you’re easily distracted or stressed by loud noises (it’s the kitchen exhaust fan for me), bright artificial lighting, uncomfortable clothing, or other people’s moods. If so, you may be among the 30% of people who are highly sensitive to sensory input from the environment.

We all navigate the world using our senses. It’s just that some of us seem to take in more and be more impacted by what we take in. Scientists are still making discoveries about sensory processing in different situations and for different people.

Recent findings suggest that here’s a fascinating example — did you know that human hands can sense the presence of something without touching it? Last year, a group of researchers published the first study demonstrating remote sensing in humans (Chen, Crucianelli, Versace, & Jamone, 2025). Participants in their study were able to detect that an object was buried in sand when their fingers were still 6.9 cm away from the object. How? Humans can perceive subtle changes in the sand caused by the object. What’s even more incredible is that humans were 30% more accurate than robotic sensors. Specifically, the robotic sensors had more false positives (“sensing” an object when there was not one). The researchers suspect humans are better able to interpret touch sensations because our nervous systems are designed to filter noise, weigh uncertainty, and make decisions about ambiguous situations.

Recent findings suggest that clearly, there's still a lot to learn about sensory processing in humans. These days, it’s widely accepted that some of us are more sensitive to the environment than others. As we understand more about sensory sensitivity, more research is focusing on an idea intuitive to many of us: sensory processing sensitivity comes with great benefits.

Dr. Elaine Aron began researching sensory processing sensitivity (SPS; also called high sensitivity) in 1991. SPS is well summarized as “lower sensory thresholds, susceptibility to overstimulation, deeper processing of environmental information, heightened emotional and physiological reactivity, and increased awareness of subtle stimuli” (Weyn, Greven, Schmidt, Gillebert, 2025).

Recent findings suggest that SPS isn't a diagnosis. It's a normally distributed personality trait or aspect of temperament. This means we all fall somewhere on the sensitivity continuum. While 20-30% of us are highly sensitive, 40-50% of us are moderately sensitive, and 20-30% of us have low sensitivity (Lionetti et al. 2018). Evolutionary theories suggest there is an advantage for humans if some of us (not too many) are highly sensitive (Greven et al. 2019).

It has been revealed that sensory sensitivity is heritable. Studies have found that 47% of the variability in sensory sensitivity is explained by genetics (Assary, 2020). It’s also biologically based. Neuroimaging studies have found that folks with SPS have greater activation in brain areas involved in sensory processing (e.g., awareness, integration, empathy, preparation for action, higher-order visual processing).

Sensory processing sensitivity is typically measured using the Highly Sensitive Person Scale, which was revised earlier this year (Pluess et al. 2026). It's an 18-item questionnaire that captures six domains of sensitivity: 1. sensitivity to details 2. depth of processing 3. social sensitivity 4. sensitivity to positive experiences 5. emotional reactivity and 6. overstimulation.

If you (or someone you’re close to) has high sensory sensitivity, you don’t need me to tell you about its challenges, which can include overstimulation, exhaustion, and stress. What might not be top of mind are the benefits that can come along with high SPS. You may be surprised to learn that folks who have high SPS may actually be better positioned to thrive in supportive, positive environments (Damatac et al. 2025).

According to recent reports, if you’re someone who is more easily overstimulated by unpleasant sensory input like the kitchen fan, you’re likely also more easily positively influenced by positive input such as a view of the gorgeous fall leaves. And the positive benefit is likely to be longer-lasting. This makes logical sense. It’s also been supported by the research. In one example, Lionette et al. (2018) found that folks who had high SPS had a more positive response to happy video clips as compared with people who had lower sensory sensitivity. Research has also found that folks with high SPS can actually experience more benefit from psychological interventions and social support as compared with people with lower SPS (Damatac, et al. 2025; Nocentini, Menesini, & Pluess 2018).

In a recent development, this sensitivity to positive experiences overlaps with another dimension of SPS — aesthetic sensitivity. Aesthetic sensitivity describes the deep emotional and physiological response to beauty, art, and nature often experienced by folks who are highly sensitive.

Chacón et al. (2024) found aesthetic sensitivity among folks with high SPS strongly correlated with the personality traits openness and agreeableness (a replication of previous findings), as well as adaptive coping strategies including emotional expression and regulation. They found that folks with high SPS and high aesthetic sensitivity more effectively navigated emotionally dysregulating challenges in daily living, such as problematic situations at work.

Another recent study found that folks with sensory sensitivity demonstrated higher cognitive flexibility, which is associated with adaptive coping and problem-solving (Shippers, Hoogman & Greven, 2025). The study also found that folks with high SPS who were more sensitive to aesthetic beauty scored higher on measures of curiosity and humor.

If you’re highly sensitive, you're likely more inclined toward creativity and empathy. Laros-van Gorkom et al. (2025) found that folks with high sensory sensitivity are more likely to be more empathic and more likely to have creative ideas. In their study, folks with high aesthetic sensitivity were more likely to engage in creative activities.

Recent findings suggest that those of us who have high sensory sensitivity experience awe more frequently. For example, Dunne et al (2024) found that folks with high SPS were more likely to experience a profound emotional and physiological response to the beauty of nature. This experience of awe directs attention away from ourselves and toward our natural surroundings, which deepens our connection to the natural world. The experience of awe is widely known to enhance well-being.

This rally around the advantages of SPS is extremely encouraging. It confirms that sensory sensitivity can be a strength promoting well-being. In positive environments, folks with SPS are actually uniquely positioned to flourish.

#98355. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health
